articles.title: All cells have the capacity to time.
articles.abstract: Temporal patterns of experiences dictate the depths and rates of learning, forgetting, and extinction but the biological processes involved are fundamentally unknown. Kukushkin et al. (2024) demonstrate that nonneuronal cells in culture can provide a molecular read out of temporal differences in stimulation patterns and therefore provide a tractable model system with which to rigorously investigate how cells time.

articles.title: Static outcomes: Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation at Fp3 or P3 does not modulate perceptual learning as indexed by the intermixed-blocked effect.
articles.abstract: Perceptual learning can be defined as a relatively permanent change in discrimination performance as a result of experience or exposure. One key index of perceptual learning is the intermixed-blocked effect in which exposure to two ambiguous or perceptually similar stimuli (i.e., AX and BX) exposed in an intermixed fashion (AX, BX, AX, BX, AX, BX) produces enhanced discrimination performance compared with blocked exposure (AX, AX, AX, BX, BX, BX). Previous imaging data have implicated multiple brain regions in the intermixed-blocked effect. In the present study, transcranial direct current stimulation was used to explore the causal relationship of two regions, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), to performance. A mixed, double-blind, design administered two online sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation (active and sham) to 48 participants, although they viewed pairs of similar stimuli. Half of the participants received active stimulation to the DLPFC, and the other half to the PPC. Anodal stimulation in either the DLPFC or the PPC provided no modulation of discrimination performance relative to sham stimulation. These results potentially question the generality of the interpretation of other studies in which stimulation of these areas does impact on other indices of perceptual learning.

articles.title: Crashing the tea party: Imagining alternative explanations.
articles.abstract: Bastos and Krupenye (2026, Science, 391: 583-586) present an innovative series of studies in which they explore the capacity of a single enculturated bonobo, Kanzi, to represent pretend objects-in other words-"imagination." Their experiments involved pantomimed actions of pouring and emptying juice or placing and dumping out grapes from transparent cups or bowls and asking Kanzi to indicate where the juice or grape would remain, indicating that he was tracking an imagined object, but they failed to account for cuing or alternative explanations.

articles.title: Language learning in canines and toddlers: Shared origins?
articles.abstract: Dror et al. (2026) report that a subset of dogs identified as Gifted Word Learners successfully learn novel object labels through overheard speech, similar to human toddlers in prior work. In this piece, we review parallels between the canine and toddler findings while also highlighting important questions raised by this work that need to be addressed prior to concluding common evolutionary origins of language learning.

articles.title: The role of outcome affective value in driving human Pavlovian learning.
articles.abstract: Understanding how outcome affective value influences Pavlovian learning is critical for elucidating the mechanisms underlying human emotional learning. In this study, participants completed a Pavlovian conditioning task involving outcomes varying in their level of aversiveness: a tactile (nonaversive) or painful (aversive) shock, and no-shock. Skin conductance responses (SCRs), explicit pleasantness ratings of each CS, and CS-outcome contingency ratings were recorded. Although both painful and tactile outcomes elicited unconditioned SCRs, with greater responses for the former, only the painful outcome triggered anticipatory conditioned SCRs and robust prediction error-related SCRs following its unexpected omission. Computational modeling, through a Rescorla-Wagner model, revealed that prediction errors estimated by the model significantly predicted SCRs following painful outcome omissions, confirming their role as prediction error signals. In addition, the model-derived outcome sensitivity parameter, reflecting the affective value assigned to the different outcomes by each participant, was higher for painful than tactile stimuli, effectively discriminating between them, whereas learning rates did not differ across outcomes. These findings refine our understanding of emotional learning by showing how the affective value of the outcome shapes the predictive mechanisms underlying conditioned responding, as revealed through converging autonomic, explicit, and computational modeling evidence.

articles.title: Time does the teaching.
articles.abstract: Despite the observation that temporal variables (e.g., the time between rewards) modulate the speed of associative learning, dopamine-based learning models have largely treated learning rate as a free parameter, and neither behavioral nor neural theories have quantitatively described this link. Burke et al. (2026) rigorously demonstrated that the rate of behavioral and dopaminergic cue-reward learning scales proportionally, and directly, with the interreward interval, revealing implications for how learning rate is formalized in both behavioral and dopamine-based models.

articles.title: The conditioning-delay gradient, not impulsivity, accounts for apparent steep delay discounting in monkeys (Macaca mulatta).
articles.abstract: Nonhuman animals, like humans, often prefer smaller immediate reward over larger delayed reward, suggesting "discounting" of future reward. In studies of nonhuman animals, this preference is measured by offering repeated choices between icons resulting in smaller immediate or larger delayed reward. One possible mechanism driving discounting behavior is that subjects forget during the delay to reinforcement which option they chose at the beginning of the trial. If this account is correct, preventing forgetting should decrease apparent discounting. In Experiment 1, we tested this hypothesis by having monkeys choose between immediate and delayed reward with either a blank delay to reinforcement or with the chosen icon visible during the delay such that the icon could potentially remind monkeys of their choice. When the chosen icon remained visible, apparent discounting was significantly reduced. This result suggested that reminding was effective. However, keeping the chosen icon visible during the delay also meant that the icon was visible immediately prior to reward, potentially causing the icon to accrue more associative strength with reward than would occur when there was a temporal gap between the icon and reward. Experiment 2 distinguished between reminding and associative learning by hiding the icon after selection and briefly showing it before reward delivery. Apparent discounting remained attenuated. These results indicate that the conditioning-delay gradient is a strong determinant of the choices of monkeys in delay discounting paradigms and indicate that animal models may not capture the processes proposed to explain delay discounting in humans, such as impulsivity.

articles.title: Visual search for redundantly defined target in pigeons: The effects of trialwise search difficulty on redundancy gain.
articles.abstract: The redundant signals effect was examined in a visual search task with pigeons. In Experiment 1, pigeons searched for a fixed target among homogeneous, identical distractors that differed from the target on one of two dimensions. Target-distractor discriminability varied across trials, resulting in trial-by-trial changes in search difficulty. When set size increased at test, the relationship between response time and difficulty followed an inverted U-shaped function: Pigeons responded quickly but inaccurately on the most difficult trials, most slowly on trials of intermediate difficulty, and quickly and accurately on easy trials. With smaller set sizes, response time remained flat despite large variation in difficulty. In Experiment 2, the target differed redundantly from distractors on both dimensions, and performance was compared with that on single-cue trials. On difficult trials, redundant cues produced slower but more accurate search than single-cue trials, indicating a time-investing enhancement consistent with a speed-accuracy tradeoff. On trials of intermediate difficulty, redundant cues reduced response time while maintaining high accuracy, demonstrating the typical time-saving enhancement. However, this time-saving benefit diminished as the cues were more salient and the search difficulty on the corresponding single-cue trials decreased. Search efficiency, measured as the slope of response time as a function of set size, was determined solely by the most salient cue. These findings suggest that the two forms of redundancy enhancement arise from distinct processing loci and emerge automatically when individually learned cues are combined.

articles.title: The effect of interleaving identity- and spatial-recognition trials on cueing.
articles.abstract: Cues presented before (pre-cue) or after (retro-cue) a task-relevant stimulus (target) can improve visual working memory for the cued target. Griffin and Nobre (2003) found a differential cueing advantage depending on whether participants were required to detect a change in a target's color (identity recognition) or its location (spatial recognition). We investigated how interleaving identity- and spatial-recognition trials influenced the effectiveness of cueing. Participants completed a successive same-different procedure in which colored background pre- or retro-cues signaled whether to match a target based on its identity or location. When identity- and spatial-recognition trials were encountered in separate blocks and instructions were provided at the start of each block, cueing effects were not observed (Experiment 1). In Experiment 2, interleaving the same trials within blocks produced main effects of cueing and trial type, as well as an interaction. In Experiment 3, the trial-by-trial task requirement was consistent throughout each session (similar to Experiment 1), but the more discriminable difference (identity or spatial) was cued on each trial (similar to Experiment 2). Congruency effects, but no cueing effects, were observed. These experiments revealed several key factors that influence cueing effects.

articles.title: The effects of rapport building on productivity and preference with a simulated work task
articles.abstract: It has been suggested that building rapport may directly benefit organizations by increasing productivity and discretionary effort. The purpose of this study was to extend previous research on rapport building by using an alternating-treatments design, which may more accurately reflect how rapport is established in the workplace. That is, positive supervisor-employee relationships are often established over time through multiple interactions. We evaluated check-processing performance and assessed whether eight college students would choose between working with a researcher who engaged in rapport-building behavior and one who did not. The results showed that seven participants performed better on the task when working with the rapport-building researcher during the intervention phase, six participants either preferred or highly preferred working with the rapport-building researcher during the preference phase, and four out of seven participants engaged in less off-task behavior when working with the rapport-building researcher. We discuss implications and directions for future research.

articles.title: Parametric evaluation of procedural fidelity level with combined errors during differential reinforcement of other behavior
articles.abstract: Differential reinforcement of other behavior (DRO) is an intervention used to address challenging behavior; however, its effectiveness may be diminished by procedural fidelity errors. Previous research has shown that DRO effects may be robust despite marginal errors of commission and omission, but the effects of combined errors (i.e., both commission and omission errors) on the efficacy of DRO have not been investigated. The purpose of this study was to parametrically evaluate procedural fidelity level (i.e., 100, 80, 60, 40, and 20% fidelity) in DRO when implemented with combined errors in a human-operant arrangement using a reversal design. Results indicated that the DRO was efficacious for most participants when implemented with 100, 80, or 60% fidelity and inefficacious for most participants when implemented with 40% or 20% fidelity when implemented with combined errors.

articles.title: Relative effects of four resurgence‐mitigation strategies informed by behavioral momentum theory
articles.abstract: Abstract Behavioral momentum theory (BMT) posits that particular independent variables may be adjusted during routine differential‐reinforcement treatments (e.g., functional communication training) to reduce resurgence of severe destructive behavior. Across four consecutive studies using similar preparations and participants, our research group investigated four BMT‐informed mitigation strategies: (a) lean reinforcement rates for target behavior during baseline, (b) lean reinforcement rates for alternative behavior during treatment, (c) a longer treatment duration, and (d) a combined approach including all three refinements. In the current study, we analyzed the relevance of each BMT‐informed strategy sourced from four published studies and included three additional participants resulting in a total of 24 data sets. Lean reinforcement rates during baseline and the combined approach resulted in the largest reductions in resurgence when analyzed as a proportion of baseline. We contextualize these findings in relation to BMT's account of resurgence and implications for practice.

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Intraverbal Research: 2021–2025
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Skinner's conceptual analysis of verbal behavior has had a notable influence within the field of behavior analysis. Yet empirical verbal behavior research has historically focused on the mand and tact, with relatively less attention directed toward the intraverbal. Encouragingly, empirical and conceptual intraverbal work has been increasing over the last two decades. Most recently, a review of intraverbal research from 2015 through 2020 documented the continued growth of empirical intraverbal work. The current review replicated and extended this work by identifying and synthesizing empirical intraverbal studies published from 2021 through 2025. We identified 50 articles containing 66 experiments. We coded each to provide an updated account of participants, training components, sources of control, research emphasis, outcomes, and publication trends. Findings indicated continued growth of intraverbal research, and most experiments established intraverbals under multiple control. The current review extended a prior review by providing information regarding the nature of procedural modifications and updating how outcomes were evaluated.

articles.title: Teaching Spatial Prepositions to Children With Autism Using Three‐Dimensional Matrix Training: A Demonstration of LLM‐Assisted Material Preparation
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Matrix training is an evidence‐based approach for promoting recombinative generalization in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, the time and effort required to generate instructional materials for multidimensional matrices can limit its use in practice. In this study, we evaluated the effects of a three‐dimensional matrix training protocolusing a minimal set of 10 exemplars. To address practical barriers to material design, a large language model (LLM) was utilized strictly as an instructional planning support tool to assist teachers with exemplar generation. Ten children with ASD participated in a study employing a concurrent multiple‐probe design across participants, with target exemplars introduced sequentially across progressive sentence sets. The 10 baseline exemplars, selected by teachers with computational support from the LLM, were directly taught using a structured prompting sequence. Following instruction, 9 participants demonstrated immediate, high levels of recombinative generalization to 80 untrained combinations within the training matrix and to 54 novel combinations involving untrained stimuli in the generalization matrix. Maintenance data showed sustained performance at 2‐ and 4‐wk follow‐ups. These findings demonstrate that three‐dimensional matrix training with a minimal exemplar set efficiently produces generative language outcomes, and highlight the feasibility of integrating LLMs to support behavioral programming in applied settings.

articles.title: Human‐operant evaluation of synthesized alternative reinforcement and resurgence
articles.abstract: Basic research suggests that differential reinforcement with synthesized alternative reinforcement (i.e., delivery of two or more qualitatively different reinforcers contingent on a single alternative response) increases resurgence during disruptions to the contingency. We evaluated whether these findings extended to human participants using a gamified computer task within a three-phase resurgence evaluation across three experimental groups. In Phase 1, target responses produced isolated reinforcement across all groups. In Phase 2, target responses were placed on extinction across all groups but alternative responses produced either synthesized, isolated, or no reinforcement based on group assignment. In Phase 3, target and alternative responses were placed on extinction across all groups. Resurgence occurred for groups experiencing synthesized and isolated alternative reinforcement, and resurgence was greater following synthesized reinforcement. Unlike previous human-operant research, extinction also reliably produced reductions in both target and alternative responding without other programmed contingencies for these responses. These findings may have important implications for clinical practice and future translational and applied research.

articles.title: Applying the reinforcer pathology model to alcohol use and suicide risk: An initial test
articles.abstract: Alcohol use and suicide risk have a well-established relation. In the United States, up to a third of suicide decedents have alcohol in their blood at the time of death and half of those have a blood alcohol level above the legal driving limit (i.e., 0.08% blood alcohol content). Despite the established relation, the mechanisms linking alcohol and suicide risk are unclear. The reinforcer pathology framework of addiction, pioneered by Warren Bickel, can be adapted to make predictions about suicide risk among those who use alcohol. To assess this, we conducted two crowdsourced studies (using Amazon Mechanical Turk and Prolific) that consisted of assessments of demand for alcohol, discounting of delayed monetary gains, and suicide risk (assessed by the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale). Demand for alcohol was generally higher as suicide risk increased, and discounting for delayed gains was higher for recent suicide preparations but not suicidal ideation. Further formalization of reinforcer pathology frameworks will allow for more rigorous control of variables that affect alcohol use and suicide risk both individually and together.

articles.title: Effects of Framing Side-Effect Risks for a Hypothetical Vaccine: A Discounting Approach
articles.abstract: Abstract Probability discounting describes the systematic decrease in subjective value as the probability of an undesirable outcome increases. The present study examined whether hypothetical vaccine acceptance varies as a function of communicated side-effect risk and whether this relation is influenced by framing format. 35 undergraduates provided Likert-scale acceptance judgments across multiple levels of side-effect risk presented under either absolute or relative framing conditions. Acceptance decreased monotonically with increasing risk, and aggregate data were well described by a generalized hyperbolic function, consistent with established models of probability discounting. Framing systematically altered the relation between communicated risk and acceptance, with relative framing showing greater sensitivity to individual baseline risk estimates. These findings suggest that framing may function as a contextual variable that modulates the transformation of probabilistic information into subjective value. Although individual-level variability was observed, the overall pattern suggests that probability discounting provides a useful framework for analyzing acceptance decisions about vaccination involving probabilistic harm. The present judgment-based procedure may offer a complementary method for examining probability discounting across framing conditions and decision contexts.

articles.title: A behavior-analytic conceptualization and systematic review of interventions for confabulation in people with major neurocognitive disorder.
Speed-controlled visual stimuli modulate fish collective dynamics
articles.abstract: Fish movement is modulated by visual stimulation and associated parameters, such as size, speed, and orientation, yet the regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we experimentally investigate how systematically controlled stimulus speed influences the temporal and spatial collective dynamics of Hemigrammus bleheri. Using a customisable top-down projection setup, we displayed clockwise-rotating black-dot patterns at three distinct speeds to simulate complex environmental motion cues. We quantified individual temporal responsiveness through angular movements and evaluated group-level spatial organisation. Fish angular movements positively tracked the rotation direction of the visual patterns. Lower stimulus speeds elicited predominantly exploratory behaviour, while higher speeds induced a transition to strong motion-tracking behaviour, aligning fish orientation with the rotating patterns. Increasing stimulus speed also corresponded with greater nearest-neighbour distance, indicating reduced spatial cohesion. Notably, we observed transient schooling episodes not aligned with the rotational stimulus, reflecting periods in which internal social interactions outweighed stimulus-driven coordination. Using a newly defined free-schooling index (FSI), we show that such internally driven episodes were frequent at lower stimulus speeds but markedly reduced at higher speeds. Overall, our findings demonstrate that speed-controlled visual stimuli modulate both individual movement and group dynamics, offering new insights into how visual cues shape fish collective behaviour.

articles.title: Utilizing citizen science to assess consistent individual variation in play behaviour of the domestic cat, Felis catus
articles.abstract: It is well known that domestic cats (Felis catus) have the potential to impact local vulnerable wildlife, and that individual cats differ in their ecological impact due to predation. However, less is known about how individual cats may differ in their behaviours with similar motivational involvement, such as in response to a moving, feathered object toy. Using an online questionnaire, we recruited participants in the United States to expose their cat (N = 87) to standardised behavioural assay trials using a feather wand toy, aiming to capture individual variation in response to the toy and the consistency of the individuals' responses over time. We collected caretaker recorded videos capturing cats' interaction with the object toy, and found high repeatability of all behaviours measured across trials (mean R = 0.467). We then consolidated the data using Principal Component Analysis to obtain a composite cat interest score for further analysis. Overall, we found significant trial effects (p = 0.002), and consistent individual variation in the cats' composite interest score (ICC = 0.650). Interestingly, we did not find any significant connections between the cats' interest score and factors such as their outdoor access, history of hunting, frequency of play in the home, or rated playfulness by their caretakers. Our study presents the first recorded use of citizen science as a method of quantifying consistent individual differences in play behaviour of cats, and highlights the importance of assessing individual variation when studying cat behaviour.

articles.title: Mature Vespa mandarinia larvae continue calling at night
articles.abstract: Animals produce and perceive vibroacoustic signals. Larvae of Vespa hornets generate a rhythmic "rasping" signal by rubbing their mandibles against the cell wall (hereafter calling), a behaviour proposed to function as a hunger signal to workers. Detailed observations, however, exist for only a few Vespa species, and whether calling varies with time of day is unknown. Using workerless laboratory observations of Vespa mandarinia, we recorded group-level calling and found that fifth-instar larvae called throughout both day and night, with a higher calling rate at night than during the day. Only fifth-instar larvae called; earlier instars did not. We also characterise the airborne acoustic component of the rasping signal by its duration and dominant frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first report of nocturnal larval calling in any Vespa species, providing a baseline for future work on larval signaling under natural colony conditions.

articles.title: Coffee time: Low caffeine dose promotes attention and focus in zebrafish
articles.abstract: In this study we investigated the ability of zebrafish to discriminate visual signs and associate them with a reward in an associative-learning protocol including distractors. Moreover, we studied the effects of caffeine on animal performance in the task. After being trained to associate a specific image pattern with a reward (food) in the presence of other, distractor images, the fish were challenged to locate the exact cue associated with the reward. The distractors were same-colored pattern images similar to the target. Both the target and distractors were continually moved around the tank. Fish were exposed to three caffeine concentrations for 14 days: 0 mg/L (control, n = 12), 10 mg/L (n = 14), and 50 mg/L (n = 14). Zebrafish spent most of the time close to the target (where the reward was offered) under the effects of 0 and 10 mg/L caffeine, and the shortest latency to reach the target was observed for the 10-mg/L caffeine group. Both caffeine treatments (10 and 50 mg/L) increased the average speed and distance traveled when compared to the control group. This study confirms previous results showing that zebrafish demonstrate conditioned learning ability; however, low-dose caffeine exposure seems to favor visual cue discrimination and to increase zebrafish performance in a multicue discrimination task, in which primarily focus and attention are required in order to obtain the reward.

articles.title: Capuchin monkeys can make and use stone tools
articles.abstract: Scientists hoping to elucidate the origin of human stone tool manufacture and use have looked to extant primate species for possible clues. Although some skepticism has been raised, there is clear evidence that today's capuchin monkeys can make and use stone tools.

articles.title: A parametric analysis of varying levels of consequence‐based procedural fidelity errors when learning new tasks
articles.abstract: Procedural fidelity is the extent to which procedures are implemented as prescribed. Fidelity errors involving the delivery of consequences can have detrimental effects during discrimination training. This study consisted of a human-operant evaluation of how varying levels of fidelity errors involving consequences may affect performance on an arbitrary computerized matching-to-sample task. We investigated how implementing the task with varying levels of fidelity may affect learning and how initially exposing learners to varying levels of fidelity affects ongoing performance once errors were corrected for six participants. The results indicated that varying fidelity levels delayed learning for five out of six participants. However, all six participants mastered the task once the errors were corrected. We discuss the implications of the results and provide suggestions for future research.

articles.title: Assessing the feasibility of automated virtual reality training of functional analysis procedures for preservice clinicians
articles.abstract: Effective training in functional analysis is essential in applied behavior analysis, yet traditional methods may not include adequate practice opportunities. Researchers evaluated an automated virtual reality (VR) simulation designed to teach novice clinicians to implement functional analysis procedures. Six participants completed immersive VR training with automated prompting followed by baseline probe, feedback, and treatment-extension phases. Two participants achieved mastery through VR training alone, whereas four required brief feedback to reach criterion. Immediate performance improvements were observed across participants, and those receiving feedback continued to display mastery-level performance in live role plays during a treatment extension. Results suggest that VR training may enhance procedural fidelity in functional analysis protocols while reducing training risks. Findings support VR as a promising tool for scalable, safe, and effective training in applied behavior analysis practices.

articles.title: Training Behavioral Interns to Implement and Use Social Validity Assessments of Goals, Outcomes, and Procedures with Compassionate Care
articles.abstract: Compassionate care and social validity are interrelated constructs emphasizing empathy, collaboration, and responsiveness to client values within applied behavior. Despite increased calls to prioritize compassion in service delivery, few studies have directly trained practitioners to conduct social validity assessments with compassion. This study evaluated the effects of performance-based training on behavioral interns’ implementation of a social validity assessment that incorporated compassionate care responses. Using a modified assessment adapted from Turan and Meadan ( 2011 ) and compassionate care behaviors defined by Rohrer and Weiss ( 2022 ), interns were trained to obtain caregiver input across goals, procedures, and outcomes of a mock intervention. A multiple baseline design across participants was used to evaluate changes in procedural fidelity, generalization, and maintenance. Results demonstrated that behavioral skills training produced marked improvements in the accuracy and consistency with which participants implemented the adapted social validity assessment, including reliable use of compassionate care responses, with gains maintaining over time and generalizing to novel caregiver scenarios. Improvements were observed across all three participants, and participants rated the training as acceptable, effective, and worth recommending to others. These findings suggest that compassionate, collaborative engagement during social validity assessment is a trainable skill, offering practitioners a concrete method for centering caregiver values in treatment decisions.

articles.title: High-Probability Instructional Sequence: A Survey on Design and Implementation Practices
articles.abstract: The high-probability instructional sequence (HPIS) is a research-based procedure commonly used as an intervention for noncompliance. Numerous procedural variations of the HPIS have been evaluated in the literature, leading to best-practice guidelines. We conducted a survey to examine behavior analysts’ current practices in designing and/or implementing the HPIS, and to assess how well these practices align with existing literature. We surveyed registered behavior technicians (RBT®s), board-certified assistant behavior analysts (BCaBA®s), and board-certified behavior analysts (BCBA®s and BCBA-D®s). Our findings revealed that none of the published guidelines were followed by 100% of participants, with adherence ranging from 12% to 81%. Additionally, we found that some practitioners reportedly engaged in practices not supported by the guidelines in the literature. This paper discusses potential variables that may be responsible for these outcomes. It highlights the importance of fostering sustained mutually beneficial exchanges between practitioners and researchers to advance HPIS research and practical applications.

articles.title: Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior Citations in Behavior Analysis in Practice
articles.abstract: We examined citations of articles published in the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior in articles published in Behavior Analysis in Practice from that journal’s inception through 2024. A yearly average of 2.0% of citations of journal articles in BAP were JEAB articles, with a range of 0.0 to 7.5% across years. The most-cited articles dealt with motivating operations, token reinforcement, translational research, stimulus equivalence, discrimination learning with and without errors, and long-term treatment of destructive behavior. We also examined journal self-citations in Behavior Analysis in Practice . A yearly mean of 6.5% of all journal citations were self-citations, with a range of 0.0 to 12.6% across years. The most-cited articles dealt with functional communication training, research rankings of graduate programs, functional assessment, interdisciplinary relations, and evidence-based staff training. Articles examining issues relating to diversity, equity, and inclusion were also cited frequently. These findings suggest topics that may be of interest to practitioners.

articles.title: Teaching Autistic Children to Cooperate with a Comprehensive Mock Physical Exam
articles.abstract: The current study taught six autistic children to actively and passively cooperate during routine physical examinations. A nonconcurrent multiple-baseline design across participants was used to evaluate a differential reinforcement and stimulus-fading intervention in which brief escape followed challenging behavior and demands were re-presented within the same session across 11 components of a mock physical examination. Terminal probes were conducted following mastery of individual fading steps, allowing participants to progress independently across examination components based on their performance rather than requiring simultaneous mastery of all components. All six participants achieved terminal-level active and passive cooperation across all 11 examination components. Terminal probe data identified three patterns of acquisition and informed individualized progression through fading steps. Caregivers and medical professionals also reported high ratings of intervention acceptability on social validity measures. These findings extend previous research on reinforcement- and fading-based approaches for teaching cooperation with medical examinations and suggest that systematic terminal probes may reduce unnecessary instructional steps while supporting individualized treatment progression.

articles.title: Using Behavior Skills Training to Teach Tacting Self-identities and Asking Open Ended Questions to Improve Cultural Responsiveness in Graduate Students
articles.abstract: Students of behavior analysis are taught the necessary skills to implement evidence-based practice. However, without engaging in self-reflection and soft skills during caregiver and client interactions, students and clinicians alike may miss crucial information. The purpose of the current study was to use behavioral skills training (BST) to teach two beginning skills necessary to engage in a culturally responsive practice. First, participants were taught how to tact their identities prior to engaging with clients to understand the potential power imbalances within the relationship. We also taught participants to ask caregivers open-ended questions to gather more information when developing assessments and treatments, thereby aligning more closely with caregivers’ perspectives. These skills may be among the first skills clinicians use when interacting with a client and their family, and they help prepare clinicians to work effectively with clients from backgrounds different from their own. Four graduate students in a Master of Science in behavior analysis program participated. Participants received instruction through online modules, in-person training, role-play activities on Zoom®, and feedback. Participants acquired each skill in 2 to 4 sessions. Follow-up probes indicated that three of the four participants maintained each skill. These results represent an important step in building a culturally responsive repertoire. Areas of future research and limitations are discussed.

articles.title: Preliminary Development and Evaluation of a Severity Classification Tool Informed by Objective Indicators of Challenging Behavior
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT In behavior analysis, the term severe is commonly used to describe challenging behavior, but the criteria used to distinguish severe from non‐severe challenging behavior are not always clearly defined or consistently applied. The current manuscript demonstrates preliminary steps in the development and evaluation of a severity classification tool informed by objective indicators of challenging behavior. Study 1 evaluated the content validity of proposed tool items. Seven experienced Board‐Certified Behavior Analysts rated each item's relevance, clarity, representativeness, perceived bias/inclusivity, and retention. Study 2 examined whether access to the tool was associated with improved agreement among Board Certified Behavior Analysts classifying case scenarios as severe or not severe. Study 3 replicated and extended this evaluation using two no‐tool‐access conditions before tool access. Study 1 outcomes suggested that raters generally viewed tool items as relevant, clear, representative, unbiased, and appropriate for retention. Across Studies 2 and 3, access to the tool was associated with higher rater agreement within and across rater groups. Most raters reported that the tool could have value in research and practice settings. We discuss these findings as preliminary evidence supporting continued tool refinement and validation.

articles.title: Indirectly Decreasing Motor Stereotypy in Children With Autism via Increasing Motor Activities
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT The intervention consisted of a multi‐component synergetic learning (antecedent instruction, imitation and modeling, prompting and fading, and reinforcement) integrating with perceptual motor activities (motor planning, body awareness, and balance). The intervention was provided by a trained therapist during 30‐ to 45‐min sessions, 5 days a week during school, over 12 weeks, to indirectly decrease stereotypic motor behaviors in five Pakistani children with autism spectrum disorder. Researchers collected data on each form of motor stereotypy using 1‐min momentary time sampling during 30‐min observations with each participant across three phases (pre‐, mid‐, and post‐intervention) and thereafter statistically compared data from the pre‐ and post‐intervention phases. Results of a Wilcoxon signed‐rank test indicate that participants' engagement in motor stereotypy was significantly lower during the post‐intervention phase than during the pre‐intervention phase. Specifically, participants' motor stereotypy decreased from an average of 29% of intervals during pre‐intervention observations to an average of 13% of intervals during the post‐intervention. We discuss limitations of the findings and possible conceptualizations of the behavior changes.

articles.title: Increasing Eating Rate in a Young Adult With a Developmental Disorder
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Research on behavioral feeding interventions for adults with developmental disorders is limited. We applied differential reinforcement of high rates (DRH) in combination with contingency‐specifying rules to increase the eating rate of a young adult. The DRH component used gradually changing time criteria, with reinforcement contingent on meeting these criteria across separate treatment phases. A token economy signaled reinforcement and thinned the reinforcement schedule. Eating rate and meal duration were measured in both home and clinic settings. Experimental control was demonstrated using a changing‐criterion design with baseline probes. Results showed a considerable increase in eating rate and a reduction in meal duration, maintained at 2‐ and 5‐month follow‐ups. Participant and family involvement emphasized assent, choice, and trauma‐sensitive care. Social validity measures indicated favorable treatment ratings by the participant.

articles.title: A Survey of Clinical Practices for Prompt Dependency
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Prompt‐dependent behavior, more colloquially known as “prompt dependency,” has been minimally studied in the literature. However, it remains a problem in clinical practice. This survey study was conducted to gain insight into clinical practices related to prompt‐dependent behavior, including the assessments and interventions clinicians currently employ. Participants were individuals who, within the last year, provided services to at least one individual with autism who displayed prompt‐dependent behavior and were certified by the BACB or were currently enrolled in coursework required for BACB certification. This survey included a consent form, 5 qualifying questions, 11 demographic questions, and 11 questions about prompt‐dependent behavior. Key findings include a lack of use of assessments and interventions based on published research. Many participants also indicated they employ differential reinforcement to prevent and treat prompt‐dependent behavior. This appears to be the first survey study on prompt‐dependent behavior, and the outcomes identify gaps in research and clinical practice. Moreover, it highlights the importance of additional research on this topic as well as research‐informed clinical practices.

articles.title: Toward a dynamical systems account of behavior networks: Integrating matching, disequilibrium theory, momentum, and Brunt–Väisälä frequency
articles.abstract: Behavior science has produced robust quantitative accounts of individual processes such as matching, disequilibrium, and behavioral momentum. However, research on these behavioral processes has largely developed independently. This paper attempts a step toward a unifying, dynamical systems framework that integrates these three traditions and extends them with an analogy drawn from fluid dynamics (the Brunt-Väisälä frequency, a measure of oscillatory return rate in stratified media). In the proposed framework, the matching law defines equilibrium geometry as the baseline allocation surface toward which behavior tends; disequilibrium theory provides the restoring vector field that arises when behavior is displaced from that equilibrium; behavioral momentum supplies the inertial term governing each responses' resistance to change; and the Brunt-Väisälä analogy characterizes the rate and stability of return to equilibrium relative to reinforcer density gradients. Because contingencies operating on one response can propagate through an organism's repertoire, the framework further incorporates network coupling among stimuli, responses, and relations among stimuli-responses. All components are combined into a single second-order differential equation governing behavior allocation over time. An implementation strategy based on supra-adjacency tensors and temporal-difference learning is described, and numerical simulations of an ABABABAB reversal design illustrate how the framework captures transitions between reinforcement conditions, the persistence conferred by reinforcement history, and the effects of inter-response-stimulus coupling.

articles.title: Anticipatory activity to a daily palatable stimulus is accelerated in free-feeding rats housed in an enriched environment
articles.abstract: In addition to the light-dark cycle, non-photic cues oscillating every 24hours can entrain central and peripheral circadian oscillators. When rodents receive a daily palatable food, they exhibit a pre-feeding increase in locomotor activity known as anticipatory activity (AA). The emergence of AA requires multiple conditioning cycles and persists following stimulus withdrawal, implicating learning and memory processes in its regulation. Environmental enrichment enhances neuroplasticity, learning, and memory capacities; however, its effects on non-photic circadian entrainment remain unexplored. For this purpose, male Wistar rats were reared from weaning under standard or enriched housing conditions for 60 days. Subsequently, locomotor activity was continuously recorded to assess AA to a daily chocolate piece administered during the light phase for 12 consecutive days. Anxiety-like behavior (elevated plus-maze and open field tests), chocolate consumption and motivation (chocolate binge and motivation for enclosed chocolate tests), and preference for other rewarding stimuli (sucrose preference test) were also assessed to determine whether differences in AA expression were attributed to these features. Both groups exhibited robust AA after repeated chocolate exposure; however, enriched rats developed AA approximately two days earlier than standard rats. Additionally, enriched animals displayed enhanced temporal precision of anticipatory onset and shorter post-chocolate activity. No differences were found between housing conditions in anxiety-like behavior, chocolate consumption, motivation to obtain chocolate, or sucrose preference. Our findings suggest that an enriched environment may influence specific temporal features of anticipatory activity induced by a palatable stimulus, without altering hedonic or motivational responses.

articles.title: Effects of feeding on dogs’ frustration-related behaviours during a laboratory-based scent detection task
articles.abstract: Dogs often use their keen olfactory abilities in laboratory settings to support scent detection research. In cognitively demanding tasks, pre-feeding appears to influence engagement and performance, but the effects of hunger state on dogs' frustration-related behaviour during scent-detection work has not previously been examined. We analysed overall behaviour patterns observed during a laboratory-based scent detection task and evaluated whether dogs exhibited frustration-related behaviour changes as a function of having had breakfast before the task. We expected to see an increase in frustration-related behaviours when dogs were working prior to eating breakfast. Behavioural observations were extracted from video recordings of six dogs participating in the scent-detection task. During the sessions, dogs spent the greatest proportion of time with the tail held low (85%) and still (73%). Whining and engagement with the feeder and scent detection apparatus was higher when dogs had not eaten before the task, consistent with mild frustration, although behaviours varied between dogs and these differences were primarily driven by one or two dogs. Regardless of condition, lip licking and ground sniffing occurred more frequently earlier in the day, with lip licking also increasing over the course of the study. These findings suggest that working prior to a meal may have a mild effect, increasing frustration-related behaviours in some dogs, but additional research is required to clarify potential mechanisms underlying this effect. The low levels of frustration-related behaviours more generally suggest that laboratory scent-detection tasks, similar to the present task, do not reliably evoke such behaviours.

articles.title: Caste Dimorphism in Necrophoric Behaviour of Oecophylla smaragdina (Fabricius): Implications for Colony Hygiene and Disease Management
articles.abstract: Social immunity in eusocial insects involves collective behavioural mechanisms that reduce pathogen transmission within colonies. In ants, necrophoric behaviour plays an important role in colony hygiene; however, the relationship between caste-specific morphology, sensory structures, and hygienic performance remains poorly understood in Oecophylla smaragdina. This study investigated caste differences in necrophoric behaviour, morphometric traits, and antennal sensilla morphology in major and minor workers of O. smaragdina using behavioural assays, morphometric analysis, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Linear mixed-effects model analysis revealed significant caste-dependent differences in corpse detection latency, colony included as a random effect. Minor workers detected corpses significantly faster than major workers across all five colonies, exhibiting mean detection latencies of 40.20 ± 13.32s to 50.60 ± 9.13s, compared to 122.40 ± 14.03s to 143.80 ± 17.78s in major workers. Morphometric analyses showed that major workers possessed significantly larger body dimensions than minor workers across all measured traits. SEM examination revealed distinct caste-specific variation in antennal and mandibular structures. Minor workers exhibited higher total antennal sensillar counts (117) compared to major workers (94), whereas sensilla in majors appeared comparatively larger. These findings suggest that sensory and morphological specialization may contribute to caste-specific hygienic roles and division of labour in O. smaragdina.

articles.title: Response to Hansen Wheat et al.: Additional analysis further supports the early emergence of cooperative communication in dogs compared to wolves raised with more human exposure
articles.abstract: Here, we address Hansen Wheat et al.'s commentary in this journal in response to Salomons et al. Current Biology, 31(14), 3137-3144.E11, (2021). We conduct additional analyses in response to Hansen Wheat et al.'s two main questions. First, we examine the claim that it was the move to a human home environment which enabled the dog puppies to outperform the wolf puppies in gesture comprehension tasks. We show that the youngest dog puppies who had not yet been individually placed in raisers' homes were still highly skilled, and outperformed similar-aged wolf puppies who had higher levels of human interaction. Second, we address the claim that willingness to approach a stranger can explain the difference between dog and wolf pups' ability to succeed in gesture comprehension tasks. We explain the various controls in the original study that render this explanation insufficient, and demonstrate via model comparison that the covariance of species and temperament also make this parsing impossible. Overall, our additional analyses and considerations support the domestication hypothesis as laid out by Salomons et al. Current Biology, 31(14), 3137-3144.E11, (2021).

articles.title: Hive minds? Insect architecture and informational landscapes.
articles.abstract: Fang et al. (2026) show that honeybee workers construct specialized queen brood cells with distinct physical and chemical properties that are required for normal queen development. By demonstrating that collective behavior becomes embodied in a functionally consequential structure, the study raises broader questions about the role of insect architecture in collective cognition.

articles.title: A component analysis of evocative and reinforcing variables influencing challenging behavior
articles.abstract: It is well established that both isolated and synthesized reinforcement contingencies can influence the occurrence of challenging behavior, but currently no method exists for simultaneously evaluating these different causal variables. To achieve this, we conducted a component functional analysis (FA) to examine the evocative effects of sequentially introduced establishing operations and the reinforcement effects of sequentially delivered consequences. Outcomes were compared with a multielement FA that included assessments of isolated functions and, if indicated, synthesized functions. Results of the component FA were highly predictive of the results of the multielement functional analysis. Functions were accurately predicted for six participants with isolated functions and two participants with synthesized functions. The component FA also demonstrated high specificity for one participant with undifferentiated multielement FA results. These results provide initial support for the component FA as a precise and efficient method of identifying both isolated and synthesized social functions of behavior.

articles.title: Exploring Facilitators and Barriers to Research Participation in ABA Agencies: Early Insights from the PALMS Project
articles.abstract: Abstract Applied behavior analysis services are expanding rapidly while facing increased scrutiny from autistic people, families, and advocates, underscoring the need for ethical, family-centered, and ecologically valid intervention research in real-world service systems. The PALMS Project is an ongoing federally funded hybrid effectiveness–implementation clinical trial comparing the Early Start Denver Model, a naturalistic developmental behavioral intervention, to applied behavior analysis as usual in community-based agencies across the United States. This paper examines early lessons from the first years of the trial to describe participant characteristics, explore barriers and facilitators to research participation, and highlight potential strategies for strengthening research infrastructure and research–community collaboration in service organizations using an implementation science framework. To date, 18 agencies and 113 providers across 13 states have consented. Recruitment and retention challenges prompted eligibility expansion and targeted outreach, as well as ongoing implementation planning with agencies to reduce burden and support engagement. Organizational context was examined using the Implementation Climate Scale, which assesses the extent to which organizations expect, support, and reward evidence-based practice use. Scores indicated strong perceived focus on evidence-based practice but comparatively low perceived rewards, and agency leadership reported higher overall implementation climate than frontline providers. Overall, findings emphasize that successful community-based autism intervention research depends on building durable, reciprocal partnerships and practical participation supports that align with service realities and community priorities.

articles.title: Teaching Graduate Students to Use Culturally Responsive Repertoires During Reinforcer Interviewing
articles.abstract: Cultural responsiveness is an ethical obligation for behavior analysts (Behavior Analyst Certification Board [BACB], 2020 ), yet many practitioners lack explicit training to adapt their procedures for individuals and families from diverse cultural backgrounds. Cultural responsiveness entails building knowledge, awareness, and skills across cultural dimensions (Jimenez-Gomez & Beaulieu, 2022 ), and structured self-assessment can enhance the cultural self-awareness that precedes skillful practice. Prior research shows that behavior skills training (BST) can improve culturally responsive practices during functional assessment interviews (Gatzunis et al., 2023 ), but these skills have not been extended to reinforcer assessment or to identity-affirming language practices. Using a concurrent multiple-baseline design across three graduate students, this study evaluated a combined self-assessment and BST package targeting 13 culturally responsive interviewing behaviors during the Reinforcer Assessment for Individuals with Severe Disabilities (RAISD; Piazza et al., 1996 ) interview, delivered remotely via Microsoft Teams. Correct responding increased from a baseline mean of approximately 15–35% to 100% for all participants, and gains were maintained and generalized to interviews with caregivers of autistic children. The package was also delivered efficiently ( M = 3.11 h) and received strong social validity ratings from both participants and caregivers. These findings extend culturally responsive BST to reinforcer assessment interviewing and highlight the value of pairing structured self-assessment with skills training to produce rapid, durable, and socially valid outcomes in graduate-level ABA training.

articles.title: Participatory Development of Research Questions on Caregiver Adherence to Severe Behavior Interventions
articles.abstract: Abstract Participatory action research is characterized by research questions, procedures, and outcomes that are reflective of the priorities and values of stakeholders. The purpose of this project was to use a mixed-method, multi-level engagement method to develop stakeholder-generated research questions on caregiver adherence to behavior interventions designed to reduce severe challenging behavior. To achieve this, we used the Stakeholder Engagement in quEstions Development and Prioritization method. Using this method, stakeholders developed conceptual maps to show potential cause-and-effect relationships between variables hypothesized to influence caregiver adherence to behavior interventions. Stakeholders identified 102 variables thought to impact caregiver adherence, with eight variables identified by all topic groups. These variables were caregiver buy-in/perception of the intervention, caregiver mental health, caregiver physical health, insurance coverage, multiple children in the home, family and community perception of behavior analysis and the child’s behavior intervention, the family’s social support system, and the intensity of the behavior intervention. After placing these variables in a conceptual map, stakeholders used the conceptual map to develop and prioritize research questions focused on caregiver adherence. This resulted in stakeholders generating a research agenda with 43 questions focused on caregiver adherence. We evaluated the participatory development of research questions on caregiver adherence to severe behavior interventions using multiple measures, including group readiness, group dynamics, and stakeholder feedback on the research agenda.

articles.title: Comparison of Caregiver and Child Mand Modality Preferences Using Sequential Extinction During Functional Communication Training
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Functional communication training has been found to be an effective treatment for individuals with developmental disabilities who exhibit challenging behavior. Despite strong empirical support, variables such as preference for the functional communication response modality may influence its effectiveness. Incorporating both child and caregiver preferences into functional communication training remains important to both the social validity and efficacy of treatment. The purpose of this study was to extend previous research by replicating a sequential extinction procedure to establish a preference hierarchy for functional communication response modalities within the context of functional communication training. Next, we compared caregiver‐reported preference hierarchies collected before and after viewing their child's preference data and to their child's preference hierarchies. The sequential extinction procedure resulted in the establishment of a preference hierarchy with minimal and transient challenging behavior for all child participants. One caregiver's reported preference shifted to align with the child's following viewing their child's preference data.

articles.title: Changes in Curriculum Assessment Scores Associated With Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention in a Routine Clinical Care Setting
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Early intensive behavioral intervention (EIBI) is designed to establish critical social, cognitive, language, and adaptive repertoires. The current study examines changes in scores and growth curves on the most commonly used curriculum assessment, the Verbal Behavior Milestones Assessment and Placement Program (VB‐MAPP), in a routine clinical care setting for autistic children in EIBI services. It is also the first study to examine how correlations between VB‐MAPP scores and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scale–Third Edition (VABS‐III) (i.e., a norm‐referenced measure) throughout treatment. The mean VB‐MAPP change score was 69.6 points in about 1.5 years of treatment, with the greatest change occurring between the first and second assessments (i.e., initially steep growth curves that lessen in slope over time). The VABS‐III communication domain, adaptive behavior composite, and socialization domain had moderate to strong correlations with VB‐MAPP scores and those correlations became stronger throughout the treatment process. Age was a predictor of initial VB‐MAPP scores (i.e., lower age, lower score), supporting the importance of early identification and access to treatment. Children who exited services prematurely made progress in treatment, but more slowly than children who remained in services until a recommended discharge.

articles.title: A novel method to assess delay discounting indicates greater ambivalence for delayed rewards
articles.abstract: Inspired by Warren K. Bickel, who introduced numerous procedural and conceptual innovations to the study of delay discounting, the present study seeks to further establish the validity of a delay discounting task that is able to assess degree of preference when making a choice. We examine the construct of ambivalence, which may provide methodological and conceptual advancements in the study of delay discounting. In a sample of 105 participants, individuals used a 100-point scale to indicate not only preference between immediate and delayed rewards but also the degree of that preference. Using this approach, both the magnitude effect and the date/delay effect were replicated, further establishing the validity of the task. Following conversion of the degree of preference to an ambivalence score, we examined associations between rate of delay discounting and between-individual levels of ambivalence, finding that lower rates of delay discounting were associated with greater ambivalence. We also compared within-individual ambivalence when the immediate reward versus the delayed reward was preferred, finding greater ambivalence was observed when the delayed reward was preferred. We speculate that the construct of ambivalence may offer some new opportunities in the conceptual understanding of delay discounting and the application of this work to health-relevant behaviors.

articles.title: Caregiver Adherence in Behavior Interventions: An Evaluation of Definition and Measurement
articles.abstract: Abstract Adherence to interventions has received significant attention in scientific communities, including behavior analysis. This is likely due to the importance of adherence to promote long-lasting behavior change for clients in uncontrived settings and the costly impact of nonadherence. Unfortunately, caregiver adherence to behavioral interventions is poor, relative to other forms of intervention (e.g., medication). Despite widespread recognition of the importance of adherence, adherence has remained a passive concept devoid of technology. To advance the scientific study of adherence, a better understanding of the concept of adherence is needed. To this aim, we used a mixed-method approach to explore the stimuli behavior-analytic researcher-clinicians and clinicians commonly attributed to the concept of adherence in particular, as it pertains to caregiver adherence to behavioral interventions designed to reduce challenging behavior. In addition, we summarize measurement systems reported by professionals to measure adherence, as well as barriers to measuring adherence in clinical settings. We conclude by calling for action in four primary areas to advance our conceptualization and technology of caregiver adherence. These include a need for a concept analysis on adherence, reliable and valid methodologies to measure adherence, organizational contingencies that promote adherence, and professional teaching and training on adherence.

articles.title: The Answers are Off the Page: Social Contextual Analysis is Only There to Assist Observation
articles.abstract: To reply to the two commentaries, an overview of social contextual analysis is given focusing more on the overall goals and expected outcomes based on 50 years of studying human behavior and 35 years of field or community observations. Misinterpretations occur because there are different goals in play between behavior analysis and SCA. In particular, we need to prioritize getting “off the page” and away from theories and models and focus instead on better observing both the behaviors of humans and the many contexts that shape those behavior in different ways. Behavior analysis has done the first but not the second of these, but we can use the social sciences as our initial starting points for making our observations. We resort to theories when we have poor or no observations and the recent behavior analysis of human behavior has seen both poor observations of context and an upsurge in abstract theorizing and modeling. Getting “off the page,” however, requires new methodologies for observation and how we interact and engage with our subject matter, and less time spent on how we write observations into theories. Like all “science,” our written versions are there only to sensitize readers as to where they might make observations, not to record an accumulation of truths.

articles.title: The efficacy of teaching parents of children with autism effective instruction delivery skills.
Programmed discriminative stimuli: Stimulus control rehabilitation in individuals diagnosed with major neurocognitive disorder.
A Procedural Analysis of Taste Exposure with Young Children
articles.abstract: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, obesity affects 19.7% of children in the United States, and an unhealthy diet may be a contributing factor. As part of a healthy diet, it is recommended that children eat multiple servings of fruits and vegetables daily; however, many fall short of these guidelines. Research has been conducted on several interventions to address this issue, but taste exposure has been one of the most successful at increasing both preference and consumption of fruits and vegetables. Taste exposure involves repeatedly tasting bite-sized pieces of a non-preferred food. Researchers have examined several variations of taste exposure sessions. However, specific procedures regarding how to conduct taste exposure sessions remain inconsistent. This may affect efficacy but also efficiency, which is key for scaling up the intervention. The current pilot study evaluated two of these procedures: tasting while seated individually versus in a group and tasting sessions two versus four days a week. Thirty-nine children were randomly assigned to one of four experimental groups and preference and consumption of previously non-preferred vegetables were measured pre-exposure, post-exposure, and at a one-month follow-up. Results of this study indicated that preference and consumption for the targeted vegetables increased for all groups, generalized to the school cafeteria, and partially maintained at follow-up. Results did not differ significantly when tasting individually or in a group, but number of exposures per week may affect efficacy and should be further explored.

articles.title: Attachment in Psychotherapy: A Behavioral Approach and Clinical Implications
articles.abstract: Abstract Attachment theory, rooted in psychoanalytic and ethological theories, is one of the most influential models in psychology for understanding relational patterns. Originally developed to explain infant–caregiver bonding within developmental psychology, its application has expanded to clinical contexts as a model of relational intimacy. The assumption that early caregiving experiences shape adult relational functioning has further extended its influence within psychotherapy. However, attachment theory has been criticized for conceptual ambiguity, tautological explanations, methodological limitations, and potential gender and cultural biases. This narrative conceptual review integrates literature from attachment theory, behavior analysis, and cultural and feminist perspectives to examine the explanatory and clinical utility of attachment constructs. Behavior-analytic approaches have reframed attachment-related phenomena in functional terms, though cultural and contextual variables have received comparatively less attention. In response, this article proposes a functional reconceptualization of attachment as a behavioral pattern shaped by verbal, social, and cultural contingencies influencing relational learning histories and intimate repertoires. This perspective aims to improve the conceptual precision and clinical applicability of attachment-related constructs.

articles.title: Extinction burst: An attentional assessment
articles.abstract: Extinction is not just a passive decay of behavior but an active process of reorganization. This study explored this reorganization by examining the extinction burst and its connection to changes in attentional stimulus control in human participants. In Experiment 1 (N = 64), participants responded on either a Fixed-Ratio 1 (FR1) or Fixed-Ratio 5 (FR5) schedule, followed by extinction. Both schedules triggered a significant extinction burst in the first seconds of extinction, with the burst being larger under FR5. In Experiment 2 (N = 32), response rates and eye-tracking data (gaze fixation dispersion) were measured at the same time under FR1 and FR5 schedules. Results confirmed the extinction burst, which was again more pronounced in the FR5 group. Importantly, attentional reorganization followed a different time course from the motor response: fixation dispersion stayed steady during the baseline and the peak of the burst (E1) but increased significantly in the post-burst interval (E2) as responses began to decline. These findings indicate that extinction starts a hierarchical adaptive process: a low-cost 'exploitation' phase (the motor burst) followed by a broader 'exploration' phase (attentional dispersion), occurring only after the initial strategy fails.

articles.title: Associations of behavioural activity and environmental conditions with milk production and composition in dairy cows
articles.abstract: The present study investigated the relationships between behavioural traits, environmental conditions, and milk production and composition in dairy cows using data obtained from an automated behavioural monitoring system. A total of 283 observations collected from 19 Holstein Friesian and Simmental cows were evaluated. Behavioural traits, including activity, eating, and rumination time, were recorded using the CowManager SensOor system, while environmental conditions were assessed using the temperature-humidity index (THI). Morning milk yield and milk composition traits were evaluated in relation to behavioural, environmental, and lactation-related factors using linear mixed-effects models. Milk yield decreased with advancing lactation stage, whereas milk protein and lactose concentrations increased. Increasing THI was negatively associated with morning milk yield in the initial analysis, but this association did not remain significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons. In contrast, THI was positively associated with milk pH, although the magnitude of this association was small. Behavioural variables showed limited associations with milk production and major milk composition traits; however, eating time was negatively associated with milk electrical conductivity after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Overall, the findings indicate that environmental conditions and lactation stage are important sources of variation in milk production and composition, whereas automated behavioural measurements may provide complementary information on selected milk quality characteristics. These results highlight the potential of sensor-based behavioural monitoring as a complementary tool for evaluating dairy cow performance under variable environmental conditions.

articles.title: The Extinction Burst: Effects of Alternative Reinforcement Rate
articles.abstract: Discontinuing reinforcement for an operant response can sometimes produce a transient increase in the rate of that response (i.e., an extinction burst). Although differential reinforcement of alternative behavior (DRA) can attenuate the extinction burst, the effects of rate of alternative reinforcement on the extinction burst have never been examined. Using a within-session transition from a variable-interval (VI) 1.5-s schedule to extinction, we examined how arranging different rates of reinforcement for an alternative response during extinction affected target and alternative responding of rats. Consistent with prior findings, reinforcing an alternative behavior eliminated the extinction burst. Surprisingly, all arranged alternative reinforcement rates eliminated the extinction burst and similarly reduced target response rates, despite generating differential rates of alternative behavior. This outcome is contrary to predictions of the temporally weighted matching law, which predicts both graded suppression of target behavior and higher alternative response rates with higher alternative reinforcement rates. Early in extinction, alternative responding was elevated and initially nondifferentiated across groups, suggesting that rats required some time to discriminate the rate of alternative reinforcement. Incorporating a temporary generalization-of-value across target and alternative responses substantially improved model fits. These findings show that arranging even lean DRA schedules might prevent the extinction burst and suggest potential new avenues for studying response generalization during transitions to extinction.

articles.title: A Case Example of User Testing in the Development of an Instructional Tool
articles.abstract: User testing, also referred to as developmental testing or formative evaluation, is an instructional design methodology which helps program developers and instructors refine their teaching tools and programs. This step-by-step process allows instructors to identify how individuals respond to the instructions developed while they use the tool or complete the program. Doing so gives instructors the opportunity to create desired stimulus control relations before employing the resources needed to conduct an experimental evaluation. Despite the potential usefulness of user testing, the process is not commonly detailed within the literature. The purpose of this manuscript is to detail a case example of user testing, in which a decision tree based on a concept analysis of assent, consent, and compulsion, was developed. The decision tree and 150 corresponding written vignettes underwent user testing with 15 different behavior analysts across different points in time. A description of the user testing process and the changes that occurred throughout the development of the decision tree and vignettes will be outlined. An overview of each step of the decision tree and applied examples are also be provided.

articles.title: Relational Frame Theory–Informed, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy–Integrated Classroom Psychoeducation for Adolescent Test Anxiety: A Preliminary Quasi-Experimental Evaluation
articles.abstract: We conducted a quasi‑experimental evaluation of a six‑session, classroom psychoeducation informed by Relational Frame Theory (RFT) and integrating Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) to reduce adolescent test anxiety (TA). Two of three 8th‑grade classes were selected by lot and assigned to intervention or control (n = 37; ages 12–13). Primary outcome was Test Anxiety Inventory (TAI) Total; secondary outcomes were TAI Worry, TAI Emotionality, and Avoidance and Fusion Questionnaire–Youth 8 (AFQ‑Y8). Analyses used pretest‑adjusted ANCOVA with Holm–Bonferroni across secondary endpoints; with one cluster per arm, heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors provided design sensitivity. At post, the intervention scored lower than controls on TAI Total and AFQ‑Y8; Worry and Emotionality did not survive family-wise correction among secondary endpoints. We assessed detectability using minimum detectable effects (80% power): AFQ‑Y8 exceeded its family-wise threshold; the TAI Total contrast was reliable yet below its 80%‑power threshold; Worry and Emotionality were below thresholds. This preliminary classroom‑based evaluation suggests reductions in global TA and, more strongly, avoidance–fusion following a function‑focused curriculum. Given classroom‑level allocation and a passive control, confirmatory evidence will require adequately powered cluster‑randomized trials with active comparators and behavioral endpoints.
