articles.title: Different memory systems in food-hoarding birds: A response to Pravosudov
articles.abstract: We recently showed that food-hoarding birds use familiarity processes more than recollection processes when remembering the spatial location of their caches (Smulders et al., Animal Cognition 26:1929-1943, 2023). Pravosudov (Learning & Behavior, https://doi.org/ https://doi.org/10.3758/s13420-023-00616-x , 2023) called our findings into question, claiming that our method is unable to distinguish between recollection and familiarity, and that associative learning tasks are a better way to study the memory for cache sites. In this response, we argue that our methods would have been more likely to detect recollection than familiarity, if Pravosudov's assertions were correct. We also point out that associative learning mechanisms may be good for building semantic knowledge, but are incompatible with the needs of cache site memory, which requires the unique encoding of caching events.

articles.title: The enduring search for avian geomagnetic sensory transduction.
articles.abstract: While navigating home, homing pigeons can extract directional, that is, compass, information from the earth's magnetic field. This navigational mechanism may begin with a peripheral transduction process based on iron-containing macrophages located in the liver.

articles.title: A Scoping Review of Behavioral and Cognitive Behavioral Interventions for Higher-order Restricted and Repetitive Behavior in Early Neurodivergent Childhood
articles.abstract: Common in many neurodivergent populations, Higher-order Restricted and Repetitive Behaviors (HoRRBs) are a heterogeneous pattern of behavior that consists of complex ritualistic behaviors, insistence on sameness, resistance to change, and circumscribed interests. While efficacious applied behavior analysis (ABA) and adapted cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions have been used to address HoRRBs in neurodivergent school-age children, research focusing exclusively on early childhood is still growing. In this review, we examine ABA, CBT, and ABA-CBT hybrid interventions for reducing HoRRBs in neurodivergent children two to six years of age. Using the PRISMA protocol for scoping reviews, we systematically searched major databases using a combination of search terms, yielding 392 findings. We identified participant and study characteristics, study quality, interventions used to reduce HoRRBs, and procedural characteristics historically associated with improved intervention outcomes and ethical best practices, including functional behavior assessments, assent, generalization, and maintenance. Finally, we provide suggestions for clinicians planning to implement these interventions to reduce HoRRBs in young neurodivergent children and highlight the need for additional research with this population.

articles.title: An Organizational Model for Supporting Behavior Analytic Research in Practice
articles.abstract: Behavior analysts are trained to integrate practice and research methods to assess problems, design interventions, and evaluate outcomes. This orientation reflects the scientist–practitioner model and supports evidence-based practice. We describe an extension of this model, research in practice , in which practitioners systematically evaluate and disseminate applied work conducted in service settings. Research in practice offers benefits to the field, including ecological validity and demonstrations of effectiveness. Yet survey data suggest that relatively few practitioners disseminate their work, despite strong interest in doing so. Barriers include limited knowledge, mentorship, and access to a research community, factors that can be improved with organizational support. We describe a multicomponent organizational model designed to address these barriers. Core components include executive commitment, a research steering committee, structured mentorship, group-based support, ethical safeguards, coordinated dissemination pathways, and data-based monitoring. For each component, we provide a task analysis to guide adoption and implementation across organizations with varying resources and research infrastructure. Three years of program evaluation data suggest the model is feasible and sustainable, with growing practitioner engagement and dissemination. We also review ethical considerations and situate the model within an implementation science framework that highlights leadership, infrastructure, and facilitation as drivers of sustained change. The model and accompanying implementation guidance provide organizations with a framework for supporting ethical research in practice and advancing practitioner contributions to applied behavior analysis.

articles.title: Take a Seat: The Impact of Classroom Seating Arrangements on Student Performance
articles.abstract: Abstract Strategically arranging student seating in a classroom is a commonly used antecedent intervention aimed at improving academic behaviors. This study used an alternating treatments design to investigate how classroom seating arrangements impacted the disruption and on-task behavior of four elementary students. Three seating arrangements were examined: rows, groups, and semicircles. Data collection included momentary time sampling, interval recording, and permanent product measures, with inclusion of teacher input as well as social validity measures. • Students seated within the same classroom arrangement may respond differently, highlighting the importance of evaluating individual student outcomes. • Direct measures of behavior, academic performance, and stakeholder feedback can be combined when evaluating classroom seating decisions. • Teacher collaboration can support the selection of classroom arrangements that balance behavioral outcomes and practical classroom considerations. • Data-based evaluations of antecedent interventions may help guide classroom modifications when research findings are mixed.

articles.title: Daily assessments of behavioral economic indices and drinking among rural‐residing adults with at‐risk drinking
articles.abstract: In a secondary analysis among adults with at-risk drinking who live in rural areas (N = 75; 62.7% Female; 98.7% White), we examined the predictive ability of behavioral economic (BE) indices (demand, delay discounting, and proportion of alcohol-free activities) for next-day alcohol use via daily surveys across the range of alcohol use severity. These relations were tested using linear mixed-effects models, including evaluating the interaction of BE indices with alcohol use severity. In unadjusted analyses, proportion of alcohol-free activities (β [95% CI]: -0.022 [-0.038, -0.006]), demand intensity (i.e., drinks when free; β [95% CI]: 0.267 [0.143, 0.391]), and maximum expenditure (Omax, β [95% CI]: 0.036 [0.014, 0.059]) were significant predictors of next-day alcoholic drinks consumed. In adjusted analyses, we observed a significant interaction between baseline alcohol use severity and intensity of alcohol demand (β [95% CI]: -0.014 [-0.027, -0.001]) and Omax (β [95% CI]: 0.005 [0.000, 0.010]) wherein there was a stronger relations between the BE measure and next-day drinking among lower and higher alcohol use severities, respectively. These results support the inclusion of BE measures in daily survey research to support digital and potentially just-in-time adaptive interventions.

articles.title: Bidirectional relations of alcohol demand with alcohol use and problems in community adults: Findings from a longitudinal observational cohort study
articles.abstract: Abstract Behavioral economic theory posits that the relative reinforcing value of alcohol (i.e., demand) prospectively predicts alcohol use behaviors, although this has rarely been examined longitudinally. This study examined bidirectional associations of alcohol demand with alcohol use and problems over time. Community adults ( N = 1,395; M age = 34.32, 59.93% female) completed measures of alcohol demand, alcohol use, and alcohol‐related problems in three assessments, spaced 6 months apart. Random‐intercept cross‐lagged panel analyses modeled time‐invariant and reciprocal time‐varying associations of alcohol demand indices with alcohol use and problems. Between participants, we observed large, positive associations of demand intensity (i.e., consumption at zero cost), demand elasticity (i.e., price sensitivity), O max, (i.e., maximum expenditure), and breakpoint (i.e., price suppressing consumption to zero) with alcohol use and problems. Within participants, lower elasticity forecasted greater alcohol use and problems, with the latter also forecasted by higher O max ; reciprocally, lower elasticity and higher O max were each forecasted by greater alcohol use. Breakpoint exhibited inconsistent within‐person associations with alcohol use and problems, and intensity was only forecasted by changes in alcohol use. Results support an etiological role of alcohol demand in changes in alcohol use and problems over time, albeit principally for demand indices capturing the elastic portion of the demand curve.

articles.title: From Nonarbitrary to Arbitrarily Applicable Relational Responding: Is It That Simple?
articles.abstract: The purpose of the current commentary is to highlight developments in our understanding of the history, which facilitates the establishment of nonarbitrarily applicable relational responding (NAARR) and arbitrarily applicable relational responding (AARR). In particular, researchers have recently begun to emphasize how empirical developments across behavior analytic theories complement each other. The current article focused primarily on intersections between children’s NAAR, AARR, and their capacity to learn names following exposure alone without programmed reinforcement (i.e., incidental naming). In particular, we argued that children’s acquisition of relational responding may not be linear; NAARR and AARR may instead interact in a complex and dynamic fashion rather than the former simply preceding the latter. We outlined specific implications for intervention borne out of our analysis and argued for the creation of training protocols that intentionally combine tools and technical frameworks created across theories.

articles.title: Tourism as a Selector of Cultural Practices: A Preliminary Analysis from the Perspective of Metacontingencies
articles.abstract: Tourism is a global phenomenon whose relationship with cultural change has attracted increasing attention across multiple disciplines; however, less attention has been given to behavior-analytic approaches grounded in cultural behavior analysis to understand it. The present paper examines tourism as a cultural selector through the framework of metacontingencies. In this sense, tourism is conceptualized as a selecting environment that differentially reinforces cultural products, and, in turn, influences the cultural practices that produce them. The analysis further specifies how tourism-related consequences function as cultural selection mechanisms that may support preservation or erosion of cultural practices depending on the arrangement of interlocking contingencies across social systems. Finally, implications for future research and practice are discussed, highlighting the potential of metacontingency analysis for understanding and promoting culturally sustainable forms of tourism.

articles.title: Increasing Honest Statements in Young Children through Presentation of Social Contingencies and Emotionally Evocative Stimuli
articles.abstract: Abstract Honesty is fundamental to interpersonal relationships and civil society. Although immediate contingencies often favor lying, many individuals respond honestly even when lying would be more efficient for contacting reinforcement. Across two experiments, we evaluated strategies for increasing honest responding by young children through exposure to social contingencies and emotionally evocative stimuli when material contingencies continued to reinforce lying. The stimuli were pictures of faces of children displaying happiness and sadness. The first experiment found that presession pairing of happy faces with honesty and sad faces with lying did not affect behavior; however, pairings combining verbal rule statements and faces contingent upon honesty during sessions resulted in increased honesty. In the second experiment we examined pairing emotionally evocative images with honesty and lying, with increasing intensity of providing a verbal rule linking emotions with honesty. Pairing was effective only when combined with the presentation of a rule linking honesty and emotions. For two participants it was possible to fade treatment with a return to baseline, during which honesty persisted. These results suggest that it may be possible for behavior analysis to develop new interventions to support honesty that do not require changing immediate environmental contingencies.

articles.title: Behavior Management Versus Classroom Management: Defining the Terms and Why It Matters
articles.abstract: In teacher preparation and educational research, the terms classroom management and behavior management are frequently used interchangeably, despite evidence that they represent distinct concepts with different implications for teacher training and practice. This exploratory study examined how faculty conceptualize these terms and how licensure coursework requirements for these skills vary across license types. Participants (N = 35) were faculty and reviewers affiliated with behavior-focused education journals who completed an online survey including open-ended and closed ended items. Qualitative analysis revealed five themes: grounding in applied behavior analysis, proactive versus reactive orientation, individual versus group focus, alignment with multi-tiered systems of support, and disagreement regarding interchangeability of terminology. Closed-ended responses indicated substantial variability in licensure requirements, with behavior management coursework most commonly required for special education teachers and infrequently required for general education teachers. Findings suggest misalignment among professional definitions, licensure expectations, and teacher preparation. Clarifying these constructs and ensuring comprehensive coursework in both classroom management and behavior management may strengthen teacher preparation and address persistent challenges related to behavior management and teacher attrition.

articles.title: Practitioner Views of What Works Clearinghouse Standards: Board Certified Behavior Analysts’ Level of Agreement with What Works Clearinghouse Standards
articles.abstract: The What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) disseminates standards for high-quality single-case design (SCD) research to identify empirically supported educational practices. Board certified behavior analysts (BCBAs) represent one of the largest groups of practitioners who routinely use SCDs, and the number of BCBAs working in education in the United States continues to grow. We surveyed BCBAs on their awareness and level of agreement with WWC standards for several SCD aspects for research protocols versus implementing treatment of student referral concerns that represent empirically supported best practices. Approximately half reported that they were not aware of the WWC or its standards for SCDs. The percentage of BCBAs who agreed with WWC-designated minimal (i.e., with reservations) versus optimal (i.e., without reservations) standards for different SCDs ranged from 47 to 78%. In general, there was significantly more agreement by BCBAs with minimal compared to optimal standards for different SCDs. The percentage of BCBAs who agreed with the SCD standards being appropriate for research protocols was 40%, whereas agreement dropped to 31% for clinical practice in applied settings. BCBAs were significantly more likely to consider the WWC SCD standards as valid for research protocols versus clinical practice purposes.

articles.title: Educational Leaders’ Learning Outcomes: A Comparison of Traditional and Enhanced Ci3T Implementation Series and Delivery
articles.abstract: We conducted this underpowered, longitudinal cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) using an intention-to-treat approach to compare Ci3T Leadership Team members views of, engagement in, and learning outcomes with Traditional and Enhanced Ci3T Implementation Series and Delivery experiences (T-Ci3T ISD, Traditional vs. E-Ci3T ISD, Enhanced conditions). Results from quantitative and qualitative data indicated participants in both conditions viewed their learning experiences as highly acceptable. Overall, Ci3T implementers in schools during initial implementation in Traditional and Enhanced conditions reported differential change in perceived confidence and usefulness with statistically significant group by time interaction effects. Although participants in both groups reported increases in perceived confidence, participants in the Enhanced condition reported greater increases in their confidence relative to participants in the Traditional condition. In addition, participants in the Enhanced condition reported significant increases in usefulness of Ci3T concepts and practices over time whereas participants in Traditional condition remained stable in their views. In terms of views on specific features of Ci3T ISD experiences, participants in the Enhanced condition valued the monthly leadership team meetings with their Ci3T coach (Ci3T researcher) but noted content in the Ci3T Implementation Professional Learning (PL) series felt somewhat repetitive across the years. Likewise, participants in the Traditional condition also valued the monthly leadership team meetings with their Ci3T coach and noted some terminology used throughout the Ci3T Implementation PL series was difficult to follow. In terms of engagement, we observed relatively low attendance by team members in the Traditional and Enhanced Ci3T Implementation PL Series sessions across both years and limited module access by participants in the Enhanced condition. In Year 1 (2022–2023) attendance declined over the course of the year for participants in both conditions, with similar attendance patterns for leadership team members in the Enhanced condition. We discussed implications, limitations, and future directions.

articles.title: Differential Retrieval of Contextual Fear‐Conditioned Memory in Adolescent and Adult Rats
articles.abstract: Memory retrieval is an important memory process, and its effectiveness can vary across developmental stages. The differential maturation of hippocampal- and non-hippocampal-dependent memory systems suggests that distinct forms of memory develop along separate neurodevelopmental time points. However, it is unclear if hippocampal-dependent fear memory retrieval differs between adolescence and adulthood. We hypothesize that developmental changes in brain function contribute to differences in memory retrieval between adolescent and adult animals. Accordingly, this study examines age-dependent differences in the retrieval of contextual fear-conditioned memory by comparing adolescent and adult rats. The experiment involved three different cohorts of rats (N = 32). Group A comprised adolescent rats (N = 12) trained at postnatal day 30 (P30) and tested 10 days later at P40. Group B consisted of adult rats (N = 10) trained at P80 and tested 24 h later at P81, while Group C included adult rats (N = 10) trained at P80 but tested 10 days later at P90. Results indicated that adolescent rats had a more substantial capacity to recall contextual fear memories than adult rats. While adult rats showed a significant increase in freezing behavior 24 h after training, adolescent rats exhibited greater freezing behavior when tested 10 days post-training, highlighting the developmental changes in fear and anxiety processing associated with the maturation of the hippocampus and amygdala.

articles.title: Effects of age at first fatherhood on parental behavior and offspring outcomes in the biparental California mouse
articles.abstract: According to life history theory and the terminal investment hypothesis, older animals should invest more in current reproduction than younger animals because the likelihood of future reproduction decreases with age. Therefore, older parents may provide more and/or higher-quality parental care than younger parents. However, the ability of older animals to provide parental care may decline due to physiological senescence. We examined parental care and reproductive outcomes in biparental California mouse (Peromyscus californicus) families in which males were paired when either young (4 months) or old (16 months) adults. Age did not affect males' responses to unfamiliar pups shortly before pairing, days from pairing until parturition, litter composition, pup survival, or pup development. We also compared fathers' behavior in an open field, an anxiogenic situation, before and after the introduction of a pup into the arena. Old fathers traveled longer distances in the open field than young fathers but did not differ in their pup-directed behaviors. In observations of undisturbed families in their home cages, we found few differences in parental behavior between old and young fathers and those of their mates. Our results suggest that males' age influences exploratory behavior but has little effect on paternal behavior and offspring outcomes, within the age range studied.

articles.title: Rigor Without Rigidity: Advances in Single-Case Experimental Design Methodology
Canine cognition
Yes, dogs are susceptible to the Kanizsa’s triangle illusion: A reply to Pepperberg
articles.abstract: A recent paper by Pepperberg, Learning & Behavior, 51, 5-6, (2023) enquires about the validity of the finding that dogs are susceptible to the Kanizsa's triangle illusion, reported by Lõoke and coauthors (Lõoke et al., Animal Cognition, 25, 43-51, 2022). Here we elaborate on the matter, providing both theoretical considerations and further data, supporting the soundness of our previous conclusions.

articles.title: Epistemic rationality in chimpanzees
articles.abstract: In a new study, researchers offer evidence that chimpanzees rationally revise their beliefs in light of new evidence, a hallmark of epistemic rationality.

articles.title: Effects of adversarial questioning on response accuracy in analog forensic interviews
articles.abstract: Few behavior-analytic studies have examined the effects of interviewer behavior on interviewee responding in the context of forensic interviews, and these were all conducted with child participants. Insufficient research in this area limits our understanding of underlying behavioral processes and precludes the development of effective methods for studying these processes. In the current study, we examined the effects of interviewer behavior on response accuracy for seven adult interviewees. Participants viewed brief videos depicting a crime and answered, "yes" or "no" questions presented in a neutral (i.e., unbiased and direct) or adversarial interview (i.e., the interviewer asked leading questions, provided statements of disapproval and repeated questions for accurate responses, and delivered praise for inaccurate responses). Most participants showed substantial reductions in response accuracy during the adversarial interview condition. Quantitative analysis indicated that most inaccurate responding occurred when participants changed their answers from accurate to inaccurate following interviewer feedback and requestioning.

articles.title: Survey of Open Science Practices in Behavior Analysis
articles.abstract: Open science practices refer to research activities that increase accessibility and transparency. Accessibility can be enhanced through open access practices that make articles and data available to the public (e.g., posting preprints, sharing data in repositories). Transparency can be enhanced by sharing data and analyses, and documenting procedures prior to their implementation (i.e., preregistration, registered reports). Through greater accessibility and transparency, open science practices are designed to support dissemination and collaboration, which may lead to increased scientific literacy. As such, open science practices may benefit researchers and the scientific community. The current use of open science practices within applied behavior analysis is unclear. This study surveyed behavior-analytic researchers to understand their opinions and perceptions of open science practices. Overall, respondents reported favorable opinions for open science practices but reported limited current use. The discussion provides considerations and resources for the next steps to advance an open science approach within behavior analysis.

articles.title: Conducting Research in ABA Service Organizations: Benefits, Obstacles, and Systems Solutions
articles.abstract: This Discussion article addresses the process of conducting ABA research at large day-school and residential care facilities from the perspectives of practitioners, senior clinicians, and organization leaders. We first review several benefits and motivational incentives associated with organizational research and dissemination efforts. Next, the article considers obstacles within organizations that thwart research projects and lessen the capacity to initiate and complete studies. A third section of the article describes an integrated model of organizational solutions to overcome research impediments, create a fulfilling research culture, and promote a sustainable scientist-practitioner orientation.

articles.title: Supporting Communication for Autistic Individuals in their Community Outings
articles.abstract: Abstract Over 5.4 million adults have autism, many experiencing unemployment and communication challenges. This study evaluated behavioral skills training with video modeling to improve communication in community settings selected by autistic participants and caregivers using a multiple baseline across participants design. Results showed immediate improvements across participants, some generalization, and high social validity. Findings support the intervention to promote communication and found that it was aligned with autistic individuals’ preferences. Future research should replicate these findings using greater staggering of intervention onset and longer baseline durations to strengthen methodological rigor. • Teaching communication skills in familiar community settings enhances generalization and social validity. • Including participant preferences ensures person-centered interventions. • Video modeling and behavioral skills training are practical, evidence-based practices. • Widely accessible technology, such as iPads or smartphones, may improve acceptability and reduce stigma.

articles.title: Effects of Video Modeling and Performance Feedback to Prepare Preservice Behavior Analysts to Deliver Compassionate Care when Interacting with Parents
articles.abstract: Abstract The practice of behavior analysis requires not only the delivery of technically sound, evidence-based, effective interventions but also therapeutic rapport with the clients and families for whom the interventions are designed. Research across allied health professions has established the many benefits of developing an empathetic and positive relationship with clients, yet very little research has addressed how to prepare behavior analysts to do so. Compassionate care encompasses behaviors that integrate empathy and meaningful action to support one’s well-being (Taylor et al., 2019, https://doi.org/10.1007/s40617-018-00289-3 ). The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of a video modeling intervention to improve seven specific compassionate care behaviors in the context of discussing a progress report with a client’s caregiver. Three of the five participants substantially improved their engagement in compassionate care skills after video modeling. The two remaining participants demonstrated increased levels of compassionate care skills but did not meet a predetermined mastery criterion with video modeling alone. However, both participants quickly met the mastery criterion with the addition of immediate performance feedback. Additional analyses indicate similar patterns of acquisition of specific skill development among the five participants. Furthermore, participants reported high acceptability of the intervention and results. Implications for preservice behavior analyst training are discussed.

articles.title: Graduated Exposure with the Interspersal of Terminal Probes on Health and Self-Care Tolerance
articles.abstract: Individuals with autism often are fearful of health and self-care routines, which may evoke emotional responding or attempts to escape. Thus, caregivers may avoid or delay completing vital self-care routines (e.g., teeth brushing) due to their children’s intolerance of these procedures. Negative consequences are associated with poor adherence with health and self-care routines, such as poor hygiene, stigmatization, illness, and potential health issues that remain untreated owing to missed appointments. Graduated exposure procedures have been shown to increase tolerance; however, they may be time and resource intensive. It is possible that some intermediate steps of the task analysis may not be necessary and could be skipped. In the present investigation, terminal probes were conducted following mastery of task analysis steps across multiple health and self-care routines for young children with ASD. Importantly, terminal probes were terminated contingent on challenging behavior, allowing opportunities for withdrawal during potentially stressful or aversive tasks. Results suggested that all participants were able to skip multiple steps (e.g., range 2–27 steps), resulting in mastery across tolerance skills (e.g., dental routines, haircutting). Findings suggest that participant-responsive terminal probes may contribute to streamlining graduated exposure procedures while aligning with trauma-informed practices. Future research and clinical implications are discussed.

articles.title: Contingency discrimination training and resurgence: Effects of nonzero alternative reinforcement rates during “off” sessions
articles.abstract: Resurgence is an increase in a previously reduced target behavior with worsening conditions for a more recently reinforced alternative behavior. Alternating sessions in which alternative reinforcement is available (i.e., "on" sessions) versus extinction (i.e., "off" sessions) during treatment (i.e., contingency discrimination training [CDT]) reduces resurgence. This experiment examined whether CDT could mitigate resurgence without complete extinction during "off" sessions. Target lever pressing of rats was reinforced in baseline and then extinguished during treatment. In treatment, all groups experienced "on" sessions with high-rate alternative reinforcement delivered on a variable-interval (VI) 10-s schedule. "Off" sessions arranged either extinction, the same (VI 10 s), or lower rates of alternative reinforcement (VI 12.5 s, VI 16.6 s, VI 25 s, or VI 50 s). CDT eliminated resurgence only when extinction was arranged during "off" sessions, but resurgence was reduced when the VI 50 s was arranged. Resurgence as choice in context theory described the data well, assuming that the biasing effects of discriminating the relevant contingencies are a function of the ratio of alternative reinforcement rates for "off" versus "on" sessions. These findings suggest CDT can reduce resurgence without requiring extinction of the alternative response if alternating reinforcement rates differ enough across sessions.

articles.title: A Systematic Replication: Instructive Feedback to Produce Emerging Play Responses
articles.abstract: Abstract Social deficits are common in children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To help facilitate the development of social behaviors, practitioners may target specific play skills, such as with toys. Previous researchers have used discrete trial training (DTT) to teach a variety of skills, including play, to individuals with ASD (Smith, 2001). DTT is a structured instructional procedure consisting of an antecedent instruction, learner response (with prompts provided as needed), consequence delivery, and a brief intertrial interval before the next trial. Building on this framework, instructive feedback (IF) has been used as an exposure-based procedure to promote play skills among individuals with ASD (Grow et al., 2016; Morton et al., 2023). IF embeds a secondary learning target commonly during the intertrial interval of the DTT sequence, typically following a correct response to the primary target, thereby providing additional learning opportunities without requiring separate teaching trials. In the current study, we replicated and extended Grow et al. (2016) and Morton et al. (2023) with three participants diagnosed with ASD. Participants received two forms of DTT that targeted speaker-responding, both with and without IF that involved modeling a play response with a toy. Overall, all participants acquired primary targeted speaker responses, and two participants demonstrated some acquisition and generalization of the secondary toy play responses. Our results extend previous research suggesting that including IF within DTT is effective in teaching speaker and play responding to children with ASD.

articles.title: Generalized Functional and Equivalence Classes through Simple Successive Discriminations
articles.abstract: Relational responding can emerge following simple-discrimination training, without the explicit conditional discrimination components programmed in commonly used procedures such as simultaneous matching-to-sample (S-MTS) or go/no-go matching with compound stimuli (GNG-compound). Findings from this research inform debates regarding whether functional and equivalence classes represent distinct or overlapping behavioral processes. The present study aimed to contribute to this literature through a systematic replication evaluating whether generalized functional and equivalence classes can emerge following simple successive discrimination training in typically developing adults. A single-subject design was used to train and test the formation, generalization, and emergence of functional and equivalence classes in 10 participants. Seven participants showed transfer of newly acquired responses from A to B and C stimuli, indicating the formation of two 3-member functional classes. Nine participants demonstrated transfer to D stimuli, suggesting robust generalization. Approximately half of the participants showed responding consistent with equivalence, as tested using a GNG-compound procedure. These findings replicate and extend previous evidence that simple successive discrimination training can produce both functional and equivalence classes and supports the notion that reinforcement contingencies may be sufficient to generate relational responding among stimuli sharing common functional properties.

articles.title: Behavior Analytic Interventions for Bereaved Persons: Recommendations Derived from a Systematic Literature Review
articles.abstract: Grief is commonly understood as the broad emotional experiences that may occur following a loss (Boerner et al., 2015 ). Even though a behavioral approach could be beneficial in developing effective strategies to help bereaved persons (Brasted & Callahan, 1984 ; Rakos, 2001 ), the current state of behavior analytic literature on grief is unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this review was to assess the present state of behavior analytic literature on the topic of grief, particularly focusing on those interventions that may help people having difficulty managing their loss in bereavement (i.e., death of a loved one). A search was conducted via PsychINFO to assess behavior analytic grief interventions that were English-language, empirical, and published before July 2025. All studies were assessed across nine dimensions (e.g., experimental design, information pertaining to the deceased), including details about the behavior analytic nature of the intervention. Only seven studies met inclusion criteria, none of which were published in behavior analytic journals. The studies implemented a variety of interventions (e.g., behavior activation) and measurement methods (e.g., aggressive outbursts), including frequent use of non-observable measures along with behavior analytic observable measures. Demographic information revealed interventions are typically implemented with homogenous samples, and risk of bias measures demonstrated experimentally weak designs. Limitations include possible missed articles and suboptimal interrater reliability measures in some areas. Since the death of a loved one is a near-universal experience (Stroebe et al., 2007 ), behavior analysts should consider bereavement interventions as an avenue to expand the reach of behavior analytic practice.

articles.title: Social buffering in domestic dogs: Are the owners able to decrease dogs’ frustration during a non-social task?
articles.abstract: The presence of a familiar human reduces the stress responses of domestic dogs to different stimuli, a phenomenon known as social buffering. Recently, it was observed that this attenuating effect could also occur in relation to frustration generated by the omission of an expected reward in a social task. The goal of this study was to evaluate the effect of social buffering on frustration induced during extinction in a non-social problem-solving task. Dogs were exposed to an apparatus in which they had to remove embedded plastic bones to obtain the food underneath them. Three phases were carried out: acquisition, extinction, and reacquisition. Dogs were divided into two groups, one with the owner present (N = 15) and another with the owner absent (N = 15). Results showed that dogs experienced less frustration when the owner was present, identified as a lower level of frustration/stress behaviors compared to the owner absent group, confirming the existence of the social buffering phenomenon. This finding is similar to that observed during a social task. However, in this study, owner's presence did not affect any of the variables associated with problem solving, possibly because dogs were capable of solving the task on their own. The phenomenon of social buffering is relevant in relation to the effects of the close bond between dogs and their owners and how this can improve dogs' welfare, mitigating negative emotions such as stress and frustration that they may experience in a variety of contexts.

articles.title: When “why” meets “how” in episodic memory: Towards a computational model of Boyle and Brown’s functional analysis
articles.abstract: Boyle and Brown's (2025) functional account and the Temporal Context Model-Successor Representation (TCM-SR; Zhou et al., Psychological Review, 132(1), 18-49, 2025) approach episodic memory from different angles, yet they converge on a similar claim: episodic memory supports adaptive behaviour by flexibly using past experience. In this commentary, we highlight this convergence and build on Boyle and Brown's framework by focusing on how this function can be mechanistically specified and empirically tested. Boyle and Brown outline why episodic memory may have evolved to support learning from sparse, non-repeating experiences, whereas TCM-SR formalises how contextual reinstatement can supply predictive information about what typically follows, allowing past experience to guide evaluation. We propose that the probed recall task offers a direct way to test these shared claims, that episodic retrieval makes related experiences accessible, and this process can support learning beyond simple associative mechanisms. The contiguity effects seen in this task, in which retrieval is cued by a studied item, reflect contextual reinstatement rather than simple associations, capturing both the integrative processes emphasised by Boyle and Brown and the retrieval dynamics central to TCM-SR. By linking function, mechanism, and behavioural signature within a single paradigm, we outline a path toward a more unified understanding of episodic memory that explains how it accomplishes one of its main functional goals.

articles.title: Evidence for timing in the midsession reversal task with rats.
articles.abstract: The midsession reversal task is frequently used to study behavioral flexibility and decision strategies in animals. In a typical version of the task, subjects complete 80 trials in which they choose between two simultaneously presented stimuli, S1 and S2. During the first 40 trials, responses to S1 are reinforced, whereas responses to S2 are not. The contingencies then reverse and, from Trial 41 to 80, only responses to S2 are reinforced. In birds, performance in this task is often characterized by a strong preference for S1 on the first trials and for S2 on the last trials, with a gradual reversal of preference from S1 to S2 around the contingency-reversal trial. Anticipatory and perseverative errors at midsession suggest that the birds rely on elapsed time since the session began to reverse their preference. In contrast, rats tested in operant conditioning chambers typically show near-optimal performance with few errors, a pattern often interpreted as evidence that rats rely primarily on local reinforcement cues rather than temporal information. The present study investigated whether rats exclusively rely on local cues in the midsession reversal task or whether temporal information also contributes to the decision process. Two groups of rats were trained in the standard task with different intertrial intervals: 5 or 10 s. During acquisition, both groups displayed similar learning rates and near-optimal steady-state performance with minimal anticipatory or perseverative errors. However, when the intertrial interval changed in probe sessions, the pattern of choices was affected also by the temporal midpoint experienced during training. These results suggest that rats rely on a mixed strategy that combines local response-outcome cues from the last trial(s) with global time cues. Hence, temporal control may be present even when it is not expressed during standard training sessions.

articles.title: An Overview of the Infrastructure of the ABA Profession
articles.abstract: Abstract The professional practice of applied behavior analysis (ABA) has undergone substantial growth and professionalization in recent years. This growth has been accompanied by the development of a range of systems and organizations that support the profession (e.g., certification and licensure, professional and trade associations, healthcare billing systems). Although many practitioners interact with these elements on a regular basis, their broader role within the profession is not always well understood. The purpose of this article is to describe the core components of the infrastructure supporting the ABA profession. Understanding the functions of these systems may help practitioners better navigate their professional environment and contribute to the continued development of the profession.

openalex_topics.display_name: Academic and Historical Perspectives in Psychology

articles.title: Caregiver Perceptions of Quality in Early Autism Behavior Analytic Services: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis
articles.abstract: • Summarizes caregiver-defined indicators of quality in early autism support services. • Demonstrates how system barriers (e.g., insurance, staff turnover) impact quality perceptions. • Emphasizes the importance of caregiver collaboration for sustained involvement. • Offers a methodology for incorporating caregiver perspectives into quality improvement efforts. Defining quality in applied behavior analytic support service is an evolving priority. As organizations begin creating professional and organizational standards, it is important that these metrics encompass consumer perceptions of quality. Thus, understanding how caregivers–close proxies to autism support service delivery–define and evaluate quality may offer critical insights. This qualitative study explored how caregivers of autistic children perceive and evaluate the quality of behavior analytic services, in the context of navigating autism support services broadly. Sixteen caregivers participated in semi-structured interviews, and data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Our analysis revealed three focal areas influencing caregiver perceptions of quality: system experiences (e.g., insurance barriers, provider coordination), caregiver experiences (e.g., work–life balance, provider relationships), and child experiences (e.g., autonomy, skill development, rapport). Caregivers emphasized that perceptions of quality extend beyond child outcomes and include caregiver support and collaborative engagement. Barriers, such as high staff turnover and fragmented systems, diminished perceptions of service quality. While caregiver perceptions of quality are multifaceted, movement toward family-centered, coordinated service models may enhance perceptions of service delivery.

articles.title: An Evaluation of Shaping and Chaining to Increase Participation in Nail Trimming in Cats
articles.abstract: Routine husbandry procedures such as nail trimming can evoke escape-related behavior in cats (e.g., aggressive behavior, fleeing the area), posing welfare concerns and challenges for owners. The current study evaluated the effects of shaping and chaining on nail trimming behavior in two domestic cats. The implementer used a 14-step protocol with high procedural fidelity. Both cats progressed through the protocol and maintained successful nail trimming in maintenance sessions, although both required individualized procedural modifications. Results provide preliminary support for shaping and chaining as an approach to cooperative nail trimming in cats.

articles.title: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) in Public Healthcare: Professional Profiles and Regulatory Contexts in Italy and the USA
articles.abstract: Applied behavior analysis (ABA), the applied branch of the science of behavior, has generated widely recognized evidence-based interventions for autism spectrum disorder, and several countries have incorporated ABA-based practices into their public healthcare systems. The implementation of professional services, however, varies significantly with differences in legal frameworks, educational systems, and healthcare infrastructures. This paper presents a comparative analysis of ABA-based service delivery in Italy and the United States (USA), situated within the broader European landscape of professional recognition, and examines how professional practice functions within distinct regulatory contexts. In the USA, behavior analysis has emerged as an autonomous profession through standardized certification (BCBA^®) and state-level licensure, a credential that acquires legal effect because state law incorporates it. In Italy, by contrast, the legal framework does not provide a pathway for recognition of behavior analysis as a standalone profession, a configuration that is structural rather than transitional, since the activities involved fall within the scope of practice already assigned by law to regulated health professions. Behavior-analytic competencies have consequently developed within the established roles of psychologists, speech-language pathologists, professional educators, and other regulated health professionals. The Italian experience documents how, in the absence of a dedicated legal framework, existing academic and professional infrastructures can sustain the delivery of behavior-analytic services within current regulatory constraints. The case illustrates that documented competence within existing professions and formal recognition as a distinct profession are separable, and that the first has proved achievable where the second has not. Certification and licensure do different work: a privately issued credential attests competence, whereas the legal right to practice is conferred by national or state law. Establishing which of the two is at stake in a given jurisdiction is the first step in judging whether a credentialing model developed elsewhere can be transferred there. Recognition of behavior analysis in Europe has taken three distinct forms: an autonomous health profession, a specialization within an already regulated profession, and a profession-led register without statutory force. Which of these is available in a given country depends on whether an existing regulated profession already holds the relevant scope of practice, so arrangements that look dissimilar in form may be functionally equivalent, and arrangements that share a name may not be. In Italy, the professional title determines the scope of autonomy and behavior-analytic training determines competence within it. Psychologists and physicians specialized in psychiatry who hold documented behavior-analytic training may supervise; other regulated professionals apply behavior-analytic procedures within their own professional competence and under supervision. Comparable functions may be distributed differently across professional profiles in other national systems. In Italy, where no degree class in behavior analysis exists, post-degree programs have been the operative route to competence. In this context, such programs are assessed on their content and on the verification they have undergone, rather than on any capacity to confer a professional title, which only the State can do. Where degree structures and titling rules differ, the weight carried by post-degree training will differ accordingly. In Italy, a professional board can define and verify qualification criteria without legislative change, as the register established by the Lazio Board of Psychologists shows, making competence visible to families and public purchasers while leaving the professional title unchanged. What a professional board is empowered to do varies considerably across countries, so the instrument that performs this function elsewhere may take a different legal form, or rest with a different body altogether.

articles.title: A Proof‐of‐Concept Study Investigating Biofeedback Manipulations During a Common Dysphagia Assessment in Healthy Adults
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Dysphagia is a complex medical condition denoted by difficulty or the inability to swallow. Although swallowing is a complex skill, strength deficits in individual muscle groups may contribute to dysfunction of the overall response. One component of swallowing involves the suprahyoid muscles, which are commonly assessed and trained with the tongue press exercise. Standard Verbal Encouragement (SVE) is frequently used to estimate maximum voluntary isometric contractions during assessment; however, this approach may underestimate true muscular capacity. A previously termed reinforcement‐based maximum voluntary isometric contraction (RMVIC) strategy, in which surface electromyography‐informed auditory feedback is systematically manipulated, has previously produced higher contraction values than SVE when applied to the vastus medialis oblique and pelvic floor muscles. The present study replicated and extended this strategy to the tongue press response. Using a single‐case reversal design, tongue press contractions were compared across SVE and RMVIC conditions in three healthy adults. A secondary analysis focused specifically on the removal of established feedback. Results indicated that the RMVIC arrangement consistently produced higher contraction magnitudes than SVE across participants, particularly when feedback was withdrawn following a successful response history. These findings suggest that prescribed biofeedback manipulation may improve estimates of maximal voluntary effort in the muscles involved in swallowing and warrant further investigation in clinical populations.

articles.title: It’s Not Writer’s Block: A Resource Guide for Improving Writing Productivity
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Writer’s block is a misnomer for behavior better described as writing avoidance and escape. This resource guide reviews several influences on writing productivity, reports the findings from behavior analytic studies, presents solution‐based strategies, and considers implementation and research implications. Publication‐seeking practitioners and researchers are encouraged to adopt these strategies in pursuit of their writing objectives.

articles.title: Dravet Syndrome: A Primer for Behavior Analysts
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Dravet syndrome (DS) is a rare and severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy that is characterized by prolonged seizures beginning in the first year of life, followed by debilitating and complex features, including sleep disturbances, feeding problems, social‐emotional difficulties, speech deficits, and cognitive and motor impairments. While research with the DS population has been primarily focused on reducing seizures and other medical symptoms of DS, caregivers report many additional symptoms, such as behavior and cognitive impairment, that significantly impact their loved one with DS and the caregiver and family quality of life. As is common in rare disease research, medical and pharmacological research often takes precedent due to the significant burden of disease. However, therapies based on the science of applied behavior analysis could potentially address the behaviors, skill deficits, and cognitive challenges associated with DS. This article aims to provide an introduction to the complex and unique characteristics of DS for those working in the field of behavior analysis, with the hope of facilitating innovative research to discover effective applied behavior analytic interventions and treatments to help individuals with DS receive the needed supports and live a higher quality of life.

articles.title: Renewal of spatial response distributions in rats
articles.abstract: Operant renewal refers to the relapse of eliminated behavior as a function of context change. Two experiments were performed to assess operant renewal effects in rat subjects with different response location criteria. In both experiments, subjects were trained to respond to a variable-interval schedule on an array of five levers. For Experiment 1, in Context A, only responses on the middle lever were reinforced. For these subjects, response distributions formed a generalization gradient around the middle lever. For Experiment 2, responses on any lever could meet the reinforcement criteria. In this case, the response distribution across levers varied between subjects but was consistent within subjects across time. During both experiments, responding was next extinguished in Context B, which increased variability in response distributions. The reintroduction of Context A decreased variability levels. For most rats in Experiment 1 and some rats in Experiment 2, the pattern of responding during testing was more similar to the pattern during training than to the pattern at the end of extinction. The results suggest that renewed response distributions across locations varied as a function of the initial training conditions.

articles.title: Author diversity in the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior 1958–2025
articles.abstract: Abstract We used application programming interfaces (APIs) to estimate gender and race/ethnicity based on names of first and last authors in 4,833 articles published in the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior (JEAB) from 1958 to 2025. From the first to the most recent 5‐year interval, Gender API estimated that the percentage of articles with women first authors increased from 6% to 33% and the percentage of first authors Ethnicolr API classified as more likely than not to be authors of color (AOC) increased from 5% to 25%, with similar gains in percentages of last authors estimated to be women or AOC. The proportion of names classified as feminine and as less likely to be White has grown steadily, but even after two‐thirds of a century of growth, these groups are underrepresented relative to the U.S. adult population, college graduates working in science‐related fields, and higher education faculty. These findings underscore the need for ongoing efforts to address systemic barriers and promote equitable representation in scholarly publishing.

articles.title: Hours Are Not Dose Equivalents for ABA in Autism: Lessons from Pharmacokinetics
articles.abstract: Applied behavior analysis (ABA) for autism traditionally defines treatment intensity by weekly hours, typically 20–40, reflecting a presumptive dose–response relationship. Drawing from medical principles of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, I offer an alternative perspective on therapeutic equivalents for autism interventions. The approach synthesizes evidence demonstrating that (1) equivalent outcomes can be achieved through varied temporal arrangements (dose distribution); (2) identical hours produce dramatically different treatment responses depending on implementation variables (bioavailability); and (3) dose-dependent adverse effects warrant systematic monitoring. A framework is proposed incorporating pharmacokinetic principles: absorption, distribution, metabolism, therapeutic windows, and adverse effect profile to serve as a guide to determining optimal intensity based on treatment goals and child-centered criteria. This framework operationalizes abstract pharmacokinetic concepts into measurable clinical parameters: instructional contact rate (bioavailability), learning efficiency (metabolism), skill maintenance (half-life), and capacity thresholds (steady state). Implications for evidence-based practice include abandoning hours as the basis for treatment planning, prioritizing response to treatment over intensity as a measure of therapeutic power, and weighing benefits against opportunity costs by balancing behavioral intervention with developmental and relational needs.

articles.title: Expanding on Ethical Spaces of Engagement: A Framework for Systems-Level Change in Behavior Analysis
articles.abstract: The Ethical Space of Engagement, as articulated by Nêhiyaw scholar Willie Ermine, offers a framework for respectful dialogue between distinct worldviews. While recent scholarship has applied this framework to practice-level relationships in behavior analysis, this paper extends the framework to the design, evaluation, and transformation of complex cultural systems using culturo-behavioral systems science (CBSS). We propose a systems-level expansion of Ethical Space comprising four interdependent components: (1) mutual engagement, (2) systemic advocacy, (3) culturally responsive leadership, and (4) power redistribution. Each component is examined through core CBSS concepts, including interlocking behavioral contingencies, metacontingencies, macrocontingencies, and culturo-behavioral hypercycles, to demonstrate how relational values can be operationalized into structural change. By integrating the Ethical Space of Engagement with CBSS, this paper provides behavior analysts with a functional-analytic framework for advancing equity across organizational and societal contexts. This model positions Ethical Space not only as a relational practice but as a rigorous system-design framework for disrupting inequitable cultural patterns and fostering sustainable, prosocial environments.

articles.title: Short-term thermal exposure alters boldness-related behaviour, exploration, shoaling organization, and innate immune-related physiology in juvenile black rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii)
articles.abstract: Water temperature is a critical environmental factor that can rapidly alter behavioural expression and physiological status in ectothermic fishes. However, the short-term responses of juvenile black rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii) to ecologically relevant thermal variation remain insufficiently understood. In this study, hatchery-produced juvenile S. schlegelii from the same spawning batch were exposed to four temperature conditions: 6, 12, 18, and 24°C. The 18°C treatment represented the original hatchery rearing temperature and was used as the reference condition. After gradual adjustment to the target temperatures, fish were maintained at each temperature for 24 h before behavioural and physiological measurements. The experiment used a between-subjects design; each individual fish was tested only once in the individual behavioural assays, and each shoal was tested only once in the collective behavioural assays. For individual behavioural assays, 60 fish were tested per temperature treatment. Boldness-related behaviour was evaluated using the latency to first enter the open area, whereas exploration-related behaviour was assessed using open-area residence time and the number of entries into the open area. Novel-object exploration was evaluated using the latency to approach the novel object and the average distance from the object. Collective behaviour was examined using independent shoals under two group-size/density treatments, namely 8- and 16-individual shoals. Four independent shoals were analysed for each temperature × group-size/density combination. Physiological status was assessed using alkaline phosphatase, lysozyme, catalase, and glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase activities. Temperature treatment altered boldness-related behaviour, exploration-related behaviour, shoaling organization, and physiological enzyme activities in juvenile S. schlegelii. Low-temperature treatments generally reduced behavioural activity and modified shoal cohesion, whereas warmer conditions within the tested range were associated with increased activity, stronger exploratory expression, and higher immune-related or antioxidant enzyme activities. The collective-behaviour results should be interpreted cautiously because the 8- and 16-individual shoals were tested in tanks of the same volume, resulting in a combined group-size/density effect. These findings indicate that short-term thermal exposure can rapidly affect behavioural expression, group organization, and physiological status in juvenile S. schlegelii, providing insight into the short-term responses of reef-associated juvenile fishes to thermal variation.

articles.title: SEPARATE, YET CONNECTED: SOCIAL CONTAGION WITHIN AND BETWEEN TWO GROUPS OF CHIMPANZEES
articles.abstract: Behavioural or social contagion is the involuntary replication of others' actions and may inform the transmission of the emotional states that underlie such actions. Interactive behavior contagion is understudied. We investigated presence, timing, and networking of social contagion in adult chimpanzees, for aggression, allogrooming, and social play (target behaviours). We extracted 118.5 hrs of observational data from videos recorded simultaneously on two captive chimpanzee groups in visual/acoustic contact, housed at Mona Foundation (Spain). When a chimpanzee (trigger) started a target behaviour, we recorded which individuals (in-group/out-group) detected it (detection/non-detection condition) and whether and when they performed the same behaviour within 3-min. Grooming and aggression contagion were present and peaked in the first two minutes whereas play contagion occurred at comparable rates across all minutes. Aggression tended to be more contagious within groups. Grooming and aggression contagion were highest in young adults and -for aggression- in males. Aggression can propagate within groups and young adults can form alliances via grooming and - especially if males - compete for dominant positions. Low play contagion in adults may explain why it was no modulation factor emerged. Social network analyses suggested a double valence of social play because individual Eigenvector centrality values in the play and aggression contagion networks were positively correlated, and a correlation trend was found between play and grooming contagion networks. This study, focusing on chimpanzees as our closest relatives, sheds light on the biological roots of behaviour transmission and potentially the emotions (linked to arousal, care, reward systems) behind it.

articles.title: Experimental evidence for voluntary vocal control in an aged Pacific white-sided dolphin
articles.abstract: Voluntary vocal control is a fundamental component underlying vocal learning in animals. However, quantitative reports on the establishment of voluntary vocal control during training have been limited. In this study, we experimentally examined the trainability of voluntary vocal control in an aged male Pacific white-sided dolphin via operant conditioning with differential reinforcement of vocal responses. The dolphin was trained to suppress vocalizations during a standby condition and to selectively produce two call types (burst and chorus) in response to two distinct visual cues. Importantly, the learning process of the chorus, which the dolphin had not previously been trained to produce in response to cues, was evaluated. The learning criterion was reached after 30 training days and 42 sessions over a 126-day period, corresponding to approximately 1.5-2.5 h of systematic training. Results from the test phase demonstrated that the individual could voluntarily produce specific call types or suppress vocalizations in response to visual cues. These findings provide quantitative evidence of voluntary vocal control, a fundamental component of vocal usage learning, in an aged Pacific white-sided dolphin.

articles.title: Age-related reduction of hemispheric asymmetry by pigeons: A behavioral and FDG-PET imaging investigation of visual discrimination
articles.abstract: Pigeons are long-lived and slowly aging animals that present a distinct opportunity to further our understanding of age-related brain changes. Generally, for pigeons, the left hemisphere contributes to discrimination of local information, whereas the right contributes to processing of global information. The function of each hemisphere may be examined by covering one eye, as the optic nerves decussate almost completely in birds, directing the majority of visual information to the contralateral hemisphere. Using this eye-capping technique, we investigated pigeons' ability to select grains from among grit while under binocular and monocular viewing conditions, across three different age groups. Prior to the grit-grain discrimination task, pigeons were injected with a radioactive tracer, which was taken up by the brain as the pigeons performed the task. Upon completion of the discrimination task, the pigeons' brains were imaged via [18F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scans. This process allowed us to compare hemispheric activity during the discrimination task for each individual within each age group. The Very Old subjects showed significantly worse discrimination performance compared to the Adult and Old subjects, particularly when needing to search primarily with their right hemisphere. Furthermore, the Very Old subjects did not show differences in hemispheric activation when performing the task, whereas the left hemisphere was most active for the Adult and Old groups. To our knowledge, this is the first study to use FDG-PET imaging to evaluate whether the pigeon brain shows evidence of age-related reduction in hemispheric asymmetry during a visual discrimination task.

articles.title: Involvement of the neural social behaviour network during social information acquisition in zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata)
articles.abstract: Female zebra finches Taeniopygia guttata will copy the novel foraging choice of males. The degree to which they do so, however, can vary considerably. Among-individual differences in social learning and their underlying neural pathways have received relatively little attention and remain poorly understood. Here, then, we allowed female zebra finches to observe live-streamed male demonstrators feeding from one of two novel-coloured feeders (social information acquisition phase). After this social information acquisition phase, we tested from which feeder the females preferred to feed to determine whether they copied the feeder choice of the male demonstrator (social learning test phase). We then examined the brains of these females for immediate early gene activity (c-fos) in the neural social behaviour network for the time during which they were observing the male feeding. Of the 12 regions and sub-regions in the brain examined we found only one weak correlation: greater copying was associated with lower activity in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, BSTmv. Future work should perhaps focus on neural activity that occurs during the stage in which there is evidence that animals have copied a demonstrator (i.e., social learning test phase in the current experiment) rather than during the period in which those animals observe that demonstrator (i.e., social information acquisition phase in the current experiment). What is clear is that the considerable emphasis on examining the behavioural component of social learning has not yet been accompanied by neural analyses.

articles.title: The choose-short and choose-long effects may depend on interval consistency and similarity
articles.abstract: The present study examined the effects of varying the events occurring during the delay interval (DI) and the intertrial interval (ITI) on asymmetries in temporal discrimination in pigeons. Four groups were exposed to combinations of equal or different events during DIs and ITIs and consistent or inconsistent arrangements between short-sample and long-sample trials. Results showed that differentiating short from long samples shortened acquisition time and eliminated asymmetries in performance. The specific form of performance depended on the interaction between interval similarity and task arrangement: Equal intervals with consistent arrangements produced a choose-short effect, whereas different intervals with consistent arrangements produced a choose-long effect. Inconsistent arrangements led to symmetrical performance, either stable or decreasing as the DI increased. These findings indicate that asymmetries in temporal discrimination under delayed matching-to-sample procedures depend not on memory mechanisms such as code loss or subjective shortening, but on how the organization of task events within the delay and intertrial intervals enhances or reduces stimulus control. The study thus supports interpreting temporal discrimination in this class of procedures as a problem of stimulus control shaped by the task's event structure rather than by memory decay.

articles.title: Associative changes in human learning when cues with different learning histories are trained in compound.
articles.abstract: The present experiments investigated associative changes during compound training involving cues with different learning histories. Across three human predictive learning experiments using the compound test procedure (Rescorla, 2000), participants learned about the effects of foods (cues) on inflammation, outcome ranging from -10 (or 0) to +10, in a hypothetical patient. Cues A and C were trained as excitatory (AW+10, CZ+10), whereas cues B and D as inhibitory (X+10 XB0 XD0 in Experiments 1 and 3; X+10 XB-10 XD-10 in Experiment 2). Subsequently, participants received compound training with AB+10, followed by a final test in which outcome expectations were assessed for the test compounds AD and BC. Moreover, Experiments 4a and 4b, using a forced-choice confidence test, demonstrated that participants were less certain about A after AW+10 training than about B after X+10 XB0 or X+10 XB-10 training. If cues that generate greater individual prediction error during the compound training undergo larger associative change, BC should receive higher ratings than AD. Alternatively, if participants preferentially attribute the compound outcome to the less certain cue, AD should receive higher ratings than BC. In Experiments 1 and 3, BC received higher ratings than AD, suggesting that the cue with greater individual prediction error, and higher certainty, underwent greater associative change. However, in Experiment 2, AD received higher ratings than BC, indicating greater learning about the cue with lower certainty, and lower individual prediction error. We discuss theoretical implications of our findings for the roles of prediction error and certainty in associative learning.

articles.title: Mirror, mirror, on the … surface? Mirror-guided learning in octopuses.
articles.abstract: can learn to use a mirror reflection to navigate to an out-of-view target for a reward, providing the first demonstration of mirror-mediated foraging, and of potential spatial reflection use, in an invertebrate. We situate this within a framework that distinguishes between different types of mirror information processing (including mirror self-recognition), examine statistical and stimulus-related caveats, and argue that reflection use may be more ecologically grounded in cephalopods than an aquatic lifestyle might suggest.

articles.title: Training Compassionate Behaviors in the Supervisory Context: A Systematic Replication of Rohrer and Weiss (2023)
articles.abstract: Compassionate care is a framework for service delivery that places a strong emphasis on building relationships and working with clients and caregivers to support growth and alleviate suffering. Recent research examined the use of behavioral skills training (BST) to teach compassionate care skills to master’s students in behavior analysis (Rohrer & Weiss, 2023 ). This study sought to extend that research by evaluating BST to teach compassionate care skills to BCBA supervisors as it applied to their work with supervisees. Eleven behaviors consistent with compassionate care were broken down into three supervision skill sets: basic skills, interest in the supervisee, and joining with the supervisee. Three supervising BCBAs® in their first 0–3 years of practice participated via a telehealth format. All three participants increased their engagement in compassionate behaviors in post-training probe sessions. Additionally, these compassionate skills also were observed in naturally occurring supervision meetings for all participants. Participants’ ratings of the procedures and outcomes were favorable, as were outcome ratings from supervisees. • Expands research on teaching compassionate behaviors. • Extends research on teaching compassionate behaviors in the supervision context. • Demonstrates that compassionate supervisor behaviors can be trained utilizing BST. • Demonstrates that interpersonal behaviors can be objectively measured.

articles.title: A Graphing Tutorial for the Changing-Criterion Design: Instructions for macOS
articles.abstract: Graphs are indispensable for behavioral practitioners. Given their importance, researchers have published graphing tutorials for three single-case experimental designs (i.e., reversal design, multielement design, multiple-baseline design). This tutorial focuses on the changing-criterion design. It guides users from the data entry in macOS Excel®, to the creation of a graph, to the editing of its components. The tutorial complements other tutorials and further extends the body of literature related to the graphing of single-case experimental designs.

articles.title: Fostering Patient Safety and Success through Multidisciplinary Collaboration on Modified Bolus Placements
articles.abstract: For children with pediatric feeding disorder (PFD; Goday et al., 2019 ), behaviors that interfere with swallowing may emerge, such as expels or packs. Modified bolus placement is one therapeutic tool to target these behaviors (e.g., Volkert et al., 2019 ). This study assessed two novel utensils to decrease expels for two children with PFD and describes the multidisciplinary process and considerations to ensure patient safety. Results demonstrated the novel utensils reduced expels.

articles.title: The Women in Behavior Analysis Hall of Fame: 2023 Inductees
articles.abstract: The Women in Behavior Analysis Hall of Fame honors outstanding women who have contributed to the field. Five women were inducted into the 2023 class: Janet Ellis, Judith LeBlanc, Sigrid Glenn, Jan Sheldon, and Maria Ruiz. This paper provides details on their individual accomplishments, accolades, and impacts as described in the Hall of Fame induction ceremony at the annual conference.

articles.title: Block by Block to Success: Teaching Subtraction With Regrouping to High School Students With Intellectual Disabilities Through a Manipulative‐Supported Direct Instruction Package
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examined the effectiveness of the manipulative‐supported direct instruction package for teaching three‐digit subtraction with regrouping to high school students with intellectual disabilities. In addition to examining acquisition, the study evaluated whether accurate responding occurred after the removal of the manipulatives, whether performance was maintained over extended follow‐up intervals, whether responding was generalized to computer‐presented subtraction problems, and teachers' evaluations of the intervention's goals, procedures, and outcomes. This study employed a multiple‐probe design across participants. The current study included four high school students, aged 15–17 years, diagnosed with mild intellectual disabilities and enrolled in a special education vocational school. Findings indicated that three participants acquired the target behavior, achieving 80% or higher accuracy, maintained it for 4–12 weeks after instruction, and generalized it to computer‐based tasks without manipulatives. Teachers provided positive feedback on the study's purpose, the acceptability of the intervention, and the significance of the results. The study contributes to the limited research on high school students and supports the integration of effective instructional practices into real‐world classrooms. Implications for future research include exploring the combined use of physical and virtual manipulatives, broader measures of generalization, and contextual influences on learning outcomes.
