articles.title: Training and Professional Development in Treatment Intensity Recommendations Among Practicing Behavior Analysts: A Preliminary Investigation
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Although there is strong support for the use of interventions based on applied behavior analysis (ABA) with individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), there is also evidence of heterogeneity in response to intervention. Treatment intensity recommendations represent consequential clinical decisions that directly influence patient outcomes, resource allocation, and effectiveness of interventions. However, little is known about how behavior analysts develop the competencies required to determine treatment intensity in practice. We surveyed behavior analysts about their professional development experiences related to making these recommendations ( N = 559). Results indicated that most respondents received training through in‐field observation and shadowing provided by their employer. Implications for training and supervision to better prepare behavior analysts for this aspect of treatment planning are discussed.

articles.title: Teaching Adults to Recognize and Respond to Suspected Opioid Overdose: A Proof‐of‐Concept Evaluation
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT The opioid crisis remains a major public health emergency in the United States, with over 100,000 drug overdose deaths reported in 2023, nearly 80,000 involving opioids. Naloxone is available over the counter and can reverse the effects of opioid overdose, but responding effectively requires more than operating the device. Bystanders must discriminate suspected overdose from other presentations, administer naloxone, contact emergency services, monitor the person, and decide whether to repeat dosing. Overdose education and naloxone distribution programs typically evaluate outcomes with knowledge tests and self‐report, whereas direct measures of this response chain are rare. In this proof‐of‐concept evaluation, we developed task analyses and a contingency‐based simulation to directly measure the response of three adults, and we evaluated behavioral skills training (BST) in a nonconcurrent multiple baseline across participants design. During baseline, the naloxone trainer and the manufacturer's written directions were available. No participant met the mastery criterion and steps included in the directions were rarely performed. Following BST, all participants demonstrated mastery‐level responding across the three training scenarios, correct responding during context‐generalization probes, and returned high social validity ratings. We discuss what the current evaluation can and cannot conclude about training and the research that should follow on this socially important target response.

articles.title: Decoding diversity: Are there patterns in the organization of grooming movements in domestic cats?
articles.abstract: Grooming is crucial for mammalian health and hygiene, serving diverse functions such as parasite defense, removing dirt, and thermoregulation. Grooming is not purely reactive but integrated into daily routines and regulated endogenously. In rodents, it has been shown to follow a sequential structure with predictable patterns, often interpreted as reflecting pattern-generating neurological programs. In this study, we examined the temporal and spatial structure of self-grooming sequences in cats to test whether grooming in this species follows similarly predictable patterns. Grooming performance in 17 cats was recorded, and 40 sequences were analyzed to discern the allocation of grooming time to different body areas. Pattern analyses reveal the temporal order in which body areas were cleaned. Oral grooming occupies the largest portion of grooming time, whereas face washing and scratching were less frequent. High individual variation was found in the distribution of grooming time across body areas and in the spatiotemporal order of sequences, challenging the idea of strict patterns and grooming rules in cats. Instead, our analyses indicate that grooming is structured by probabilistic transitions between spatially adjacent body regions. We conclude that grooming sequences in cats are primarily determined by the spatial proximity of grooming targets and movement efficiency.

articles.title: Effects of positive or negative reinforcement history and extinction arrangement on resurgence
articles.abstract: The recurrence of previously reduced behavior following successful differential reinforcement has been termed resurgence. Across studies, resurgence has occurred following either positive or negative reinforcement, but no direct within-experiment comparisons have been conducted. The primary purpose of the current experiments was to address this gap by comparing resurgence following a history of positive or negative reinforcement with human participants responding to earn or avoid losing money. Across experiments, we manipulated the arrangement of the resurgence test following negative reinforcement; money losses were discontinued in Experiment 1 and made inescapable during Experiment 2. Avoidance responding persisted after the discontinuation of monetary loss during Experiment 1, precluding comparisons of resurgence. Conversely, unavoidable monetary losses resulted in greater resurgence relative to discontinuation of monetary earnings during Experiment 2. The present experiments provide the first controlled within-subject comparisons of resurgence following positive and negative reinforcement and show that the form of extinction affects avoidance responding.

articles.title: Preference assessment and reinforcer effectiveness in domestic cats
articles.abstract: Understanding domestic cat (Felis catus) preferences is important for identifying effective reinforcers that can support training, enrichment, and welfare. We assessed preference across three stimulus categories (food, toys, and social interaction) using free-operant assessments with four adult cats in familiar home environments. The primary dependent measure was duration of quadrant engagement with concurrently available stimuli. Within-category assessments evaluated preference among multiple stimuli within each category to identify the most preferred item, and between-category assessments presented the highest ranked stimuli from each category concurrently to evaluate cross-category preference. A single-operant reinforcer assessment evaluated whether the most and least preferred stimuli identified in the between-category assessment differentially maintained operant responding, measured as a nose-poke response to access the target stimulus. Results showed that three of four cats responded at higher levels when the most preferred stimulus was available relative to the least preferred stimulus. This study is the first to combine within- and between-category free-operant preference assessments with a direct evaluation of reinforcer effectiveness in domestic cats using procedures that are feasible for home and applied settings, including shelters. These findings support the utility of systematic preference assessments for identifying candidate reinforcers in domestic cats.

articles.title: An Alternative Behavior of Organisms: A Review of Baum’s (2024) Introduction to Behavior: An Evolutionary Perspective
Assessing the Effects of a Relational Training Intervention on Fluid Intelligence Among a Sample of Socially Disadvantaged Children in Bangladesh
articles.abstract: A growing consensus is that performances on standardized intelligence tests can be positively influenced by interventions that focus on improving relational reasoning. One such intervention, known as SMART (Strengthening Mental Abilities with Relational Training), consists of presenting participants with increasingly complex exemplars of relational reasoning tasks involving premises associated along same-as, opposite-of, more-than, and less-than relations. Following multiple training and testing sessions involving these relations, increased fluency in SMART is related to enhanced performances on tests of intellectual ability (Cassidy et al., 2016 ). The current study expands upon previous investigations on SMART in two ways. First, we explored whether the amount of training undertaken can predict changes in intelligence test performances. Second, we assessed whether SMART training could be effective for a non-English speaking, socioeconomically disadvantaged cohort. Changes in intelligence were assessed via administrations of the standard Raven’s Progressive Matrices before and after SMART training. Our results show that the stage of SMART training completed is positively related to changes in Ravens’ performances and that such training can be effective for non-English cohorts.

articles.title: Reorganization of Stimulus Classes Established via One-To-Many and Comprehensive Training
articles.abstract: Two experiments with college students were conducted to examine if the learning experience that produces a stimulus class affects subsequent class reorganization when contingencies change. In Phase 1 of each experiment, one group received equivalence-based instruction according to a one-to-many (OTM) training structure to establish three 4-member equivalence classes. Another group received comprehensive instruction (CI), in which the same four-member classes were established by directly training all possible relations among putative class members. In Phase 2, both groups received identical reorganization training with a subset of stimulus relations from each class. On a subsequent reorganization test, a majority of the OTM-history participants, but only about half of the CI-history participants, demonstrated complete reorganization of the classes established in Phase 1. Mean accuracy, however, was significantly greater in the OTM group only in Experiment 1, in which reorganization training followed an OTM structure, and not in Experiment 2, in which it followed a linear series structure. The results may suggest that under some circumstances, OTM-established classes show greater coherence as behavioral units compared to CI-established classes. Additional research could clarify the source of this effect.

articles.title: Does “Mutual Reinforcement” Function as Reinforcement for Humans? An Examination of the Function of Maintaining Response Rates Using a Minimal Social Situation
articles.abstract: A contingency under which responses by an individual yield a reinforcer delivered to another individual, and vice versa, sometimes has been called mutual reinforcement. The present experiment examined whether this mutual reinforcement maintains response rates in humans. Pressing a key by one undergraduate (participant) provided another participant with points exchangeable for money, and vice versa. The mutual reinforcement schedule followed a fixed-ratio 1 schedule. No visual or verbal communication occurred between the members of participant pairs before or during the experiment. They were not told that they would work with the others until the experiment was completed. In such a minimal social situation, in which the effects of mutual reinforcement were isolated from those of other social variables, the response rates with mutual reinforcement were not higher than those under a variable-time schedule, providing no evidence that mutual reinforcement maintained the response rates. Together with previous findings that mutual reinforcement did not increase response rates in the minimal social situation, the present results do not suggest that mutual reinforcement functions as reinforcement for humans.

articles.title: Proof-of-concept provider training on the Managing Eating Aversions and Limited variety plan revised.
Integrated assessment: Chemical characterisation and response of Tisbe biminiensis (Copepoda, Harpacticoida) to toxins from cigarette butts
articles.abstract: The study evaluated lethal, developmental, reproductive and behavioural effects of cigarette butt leachates on the marine copepod Tisbe biminiensis Volkmann-Rocco, 1973 . Three experiments were conducted using leachates prepared from cigarette butts collected on beaches: (1) different leachate concentrations (6.25%, 12.5%, 25%, 50% and 100%), (2) four degradation levels (Types I–IV) and (3) four cigarette brands (A-D), in addition to an uncontaminated control. Each treatment comprised five replicates with ten ovigerous females per replicate and lasted 7 days under controlled conditions. Nauplii and copepodites were the most sensitive developmental stages. Significant reductions occurred in nauplii at 50% and 100% leachate and in copepodites at 100%, with EC₅₀ -168h values of 1.5 and 2.8 cigarette butts/L, respectively. Type I butts produced the strongest developmental and reproductive effects. Behavioural assays showed alterations in light avoidance and swimming related behaviours, including reduced time in the dark and changes in Swimming Away from the Edge. These changes are ecologically relevant because altered locomotion and stimulus responses may interfere with feeding, reproduction and predator avoidance, potentially modifying the role of benthic copepods in coastal food webs. FTIR spectra showed functional groups associated with oxygenated and aromatic compounds in the analysed butts. Overall, the results indicate that cigarette butt leachates can produce both lethal/sublethal and behavioural effects in T. biminiensis , with potential consequences extending from individual performance to trophic interactions in contaminated coastal environments.

articles.title: Effects of reward magnitude on rats’ long-term spatial memory retention in the radial-arm maze
articles.abstract: Our study examined whether reward magnitude affects long-term spatial memory retention in rats performing a radial-arm maze task. Previous studies, using a forced-choice learning phase followed by a free-choice test, have reported retention of up to 72 hours, but they typically used a large reward (10 pellets per arm; 45 mg each) rather than the standard reward (one pellet per arm), leaving open a reward-based explanation. In Experiment 1, we conducted a between-subjects comparison of two reward conditions: a standard-reward group (one pellet per arm) and a large-reward group (10 pellets per arm). The delay interval was progressively extended from 1 min to 1 hr, 24 hr, 48 hr, and 72 hr. Both groups performed significantly above chance at all delays, including 72 hr, and performance did not differ significantly between reward conditions. In Experiment 2, we tested whether relative changes in reward magnitude modulate retention. Within each reward group, reward magnitude was increased or decreased for only one arm during the learning phase, followed by a 24-hr retention test. Accuracy for the arm with the changed reward did not differ significantly from that of the unchanged arms. Together, these findings show that 72-hr retention can be obtained, even with the standard small reward (one pellet), and that radial-arm maze performance is robust to both absolute reward magnitude and relative changes in reward.

articles.title: Learning in plants: A conceptual and experimental primer
articles.abstract: Whether plants are capable of associative learning remains a contested question, often complicated by conceptual ambiguity and methodological limitations. This article provides a critical and constructive primer on how to investigate associative learning in plants within a rigorous experimental framework. We begin by clarifying the concept of associative learning and distinguishing it from related phenomena such as habituation, sensitisation, and pseudo-conditioning. We then identify a set of minimal behavioural prerequisites that any system must satisfy to support associative processes. Evidence from plant biology indicates that plants possess these prerequisite capacities across multiple temporal and organisational scales. We further review historical and recent experimental attempts to demonstrate associative learning in plants, highlighting recurring methodological limitations. Building on principles from the experimental analysis of behaviour, we outline key design requirements for plant-conditioning studies, including identifying appropriate unconditioned stimulus-response (US-UR) complexes, operationalising conditioned stimuli, and implementing controls to rule out non-associative explanations. As we argue, adequately controlled experiments have not yet provided robust evidence for associative learning in plants, leaving open whether these capacities are integrated in ways that enable plants to form learned associations. By integrating behavioural theory with advances in plant physiology and imaging, future research can move beyond suggestive findings toward decisive tests. More broadly, this work contributes to a functionally grounded understanding of learning that does not presuppose a nervous system, thereby expanding the comparative scope of cognition across living systems.

articles.title: When clocks lapse: Comparative temporal error monitoring.
articles.abstract: Bilgin et al. (2026) find that rats and humans can monitor the magnitude of errors in the timing of their goal-directed actions, with the former performing better. Rats and humans use the same task representation but different task variables, which are derived from training history in humans and from recent experience in rats.

articles.title: A systematic review and meta‐analysis of educator‐implemented functional communication training
articles.abstract: This meta-analysis examined whether educator-implemented functional communication training is an evidence-based treatment for challenging behavior exhibited by individuals with developmental disabilities. Fifteen single-case experimental studies from three countries involving 40 individuals with disabilities were analyzed. Visual analysis indicated strong functional relations between functional communication training and student outcomes. Multilevel meta-analysis of aggregated outcomes across all students indicated statistically significant effects in the expected directions for communication outcomes (Hedges's g = 3.06, 95% CI [2.42, 3.70]) and challenging behavior (Hedges's g = -2.65, 95% CI [-3.40, -1.91]). Moderator analyses showed that outcome type significantly predicted effect size, whereas publication year, setting, research design, diagnostic category, functional analysis type, and training components did not. Overall risk of bias was low, although blinding risk was high. Findings support educator-delivered functional communication training as an effective and empirically supported intervention for the treatment of challenging behavior.

articles.title: Measuring caregiver and student detection of treatment effects: Sensitivity to changes in frequency
articles.abstract: For a behavior-change goal to be both useful and socially valid, relevant stakeholders must detect the level change specified by the goal. To evaluate behavior change that is detectable by consumers, we examined the minimum reduction in aggression at which undergraduate students and caregivers identified a treatment effect. Participants viewed scripted video recordings depicting varying levels of aggression and recorded whether each video was taken from before or during treatment. Across groups, most participants selected a video as a treatment session if it showed a 70% or greater reduction in aggression. Prior experience with behavioral services did not significantly affect selection. We discuss the translational utility of this method for identifying what consumers of behavior-analytic services report as socially valid behavior change.

articles.title: A Systematic Review of Tangible Reinforcers During Functional Communication Training
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT We conducted a systematic review of the functional communication training literature to synthesize the types of high‐ and low‐tech stimuli included in functional communication training and their associated levels of social validity. Our search was restricted to studies published in 2010 or later, marking the introduction of the Apple iPad. We identified 116 studies comprising 250 participant‐level FCT applications. We summarized participant characteristics, the types of high‐ and low‐tech stimuli incorporated into treatment procedures, assessments used to identify stimuli, the extent to which social validity was evaluated for applications with high‐ and low‐tech stimuli, and social validity outcomes. Findings suggest that tablet devices were the most common high‐tech stimuli, whereas edibles were the most common low‐tech stimuli, and that applications involving these types of stimuli were associated with moderate to high levels of social validity. We discuss these findings with respect to considerations surrounding the incorporation of high‐tech stimuli in the assessment and treatment of challenging behavior.

articles.title: A Behavioral Economic Analysis of the Intention–Behavior Gap
articles.abstract: Abstract The primary aim of this article is to provide a function-based, behavioral-economic account of the intention–behavior gap. Intentions, characterized as self-instructions, are best understood functionally as self-mands and instances of problem solving. When a stated intention, the verbal product of self-instructing behavior, fails to function as an effective discriminative stimulus for intention-consistent behavior, the intention-behavior gap emerges. This framework views the gap as a lawful outcome of competing contingencies involving a trade-off between smaller-sooner and larger-later reinforcers. In particular, from a behavioral economic perspective, intention-inconsistent behavior can be conceptualized as an impulsive choice, or a preference for a smaller-sooner reinforcer over a larger-later one. Two key behavioral processes underlie this impulsive choice: excessive discounting of the larger-later reinforcer and excessive valuation of the smaller-sooner reinforcer. Self-control failure despite strong intentions is best explained by preference reversal, or a shift in preference from the larger-later reinforcer to the smaller-sooner reinforcer as the time to reinforcement approaches. Viewing the intention–behavior gap as a result of preference reversal yields heuristics for rebalancing competing contingencies, informing prevention and intervention strategies that promote behavioral, rather than merely intentional, change across a wide range of public issues influenced by impulsive choice.

articles.title: Making Large Language Models More Flexible to Changing Contingencies through Tracking Induction
articles.abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.

articles.title: Unravelling Fast Fashion: Analysing Multi-level Cultural Contingencies in a Global Industry
articles.abstract: Responsible for more global CO_2 emissions than aviation and shipping combined, climate impacts from the fashion industry are a global challenge. While there is increasing pressure to reduce post-consumer waste, interventions lack fulsome consideration of the functional relations underlying textile consumption and disposal behaviours. Cultural systems analysis offers a promising means to examine the contingencies impacting textile waste, allowing researchers to pinpoint key variables to bring about meaningful behavioural change. A series of interviews, surveys, and focus groups with design stakeholders and members of the general public were conducted to examine the metacontingencies surrounding textile waste at end-of-life. The three processes of selection within the metacontingency (manufacture and design practices, aggregate product available to purchase by consumers, and group rules surrounding textile consumption) are addressed as they relate specifically to textile production in an effort to support the development of effective interventions at each level. By better understanding the selection and reinforcement of stakeholder behaviours fuelling waste in the textile industry, we can better address these practices effectively through targeted intervention.

articles.title: Treatment Outcomes Informed by Indirect and Descriptive Assessment in a PreK Setting
Introduction to the Special Sections of the 47th Annual Teacher Educators for Children with Behavior Disorders (TECBD) Conference
The Landscape of Automatic Reinforcement: A Scoping Review of Participant Characteristics and Behavioral Topographies
articles.abstract: The literature on automatically maintained behaviors has been narrowly focused on individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Yet, automatic reinforcement represents a universal behavioral principle rather than a diagnostic trait. Its relevance extends well beyond traditional clinical profiles, making it important to extend this analytical lens into the classrooms of students with emotional behavioral disorders (EBD). The purpose of this scoping review was to examine the functional analysis literature, focusing solely on participants whose behaviors were maintained by an automatic function. By examining the intersection of participant characteristics, environmental contexts, and behavioral topographies, this review sought to determine the extent to which current research is inclusive of individuals with EBD. Using predetermined inclusion criteria, 27 studies were included and examined across participant demographics, target behavior, and setting. The current review revealed that the majority of the participants were elementary-aged males with ASD or ID, exhibiting motor stereotypy or SIB. It was also noted that limited demographic information was provided for many participants. The findings of this review suggest that without basic demographic information conclusions from research regarding automatic reinforcement are limited, as we do not have a thorough understanding of the features that define them. Future research is encouraged to explore the identification of automatically maintained behavior in students with more diverse eligibility/diagnostic profiles and target behaviors beyond stereotypies and repetitive behaviors.

articles.title: Morphological and behavioural predictors of motor laterality in domestic horses: A cross-sectional field study
articles.abstract: Motor laterality in horses affects performance, training, and welfare. A simple morphological marker for laterality would help riders, trainers, and veterinarians identify likely locomotor asymmetries early. This study tested whether observable morphological and behavioural characteristics were associated with rider-perceived motor laterality in domestic horses, using a cross-sectional observational field study design conducted in the Blida and Algiers regions of Algeria. The study included 100 regularly ridden domestic horses. Mane orientation, facial whorl characteristics, standing curvature, masticatory laterality, mouth hardness side, spontaneous body bending, and preferred limb use were recorded. Experienced riders assessed two laterality outcomes: preferred forelimb at walk departure (dep1) and ease of canter departure (dep2). Univariable and multivariable analyses tested associations between recorded characteristics and laterality outcomes. Mane orientation was the strongest predictor of laterality (p < 0.001): right-maned horses were predominantly right-lateralised (dep1: 91.1%; dep2: 78.7%), and left-maned horses were mainly left-lateralised (dep1: 89.1%; dep2: 81.1%). In multivariable analysis, mane orientation was the sole independent predictor (dep1 OR = 83.71; dep2 OR = 15.91; GEE OR = 32.12, 95% CI 13.30-77.61). Model discrimination was excellent (AUC = 0.91). Masticatory laterality and mouth hardness side showed significant univariable associations but were not independent predictors. Facial whorl traits, age, breed, discipline, and sex showed no significant associations. The cross-sectional design prevents causal inference. Laterality outcomes relied on rider perception rather than objective kinematic measurements, which introduces possible observer bias. Longitudinal and biomechanical validation remains needed. Mane orientation is a robust, non-invasive indicator of inherent motor laterality in domestic horses and can be used by riders, trainers, and veterinarians to anticipate locomotor asymmetries without specialised equipment. Longitudinal and kinematic studies are required to confirm causality.

articles.title: Strong preference of conspecific odour is not altered by pre-habituation in Black Rats (Rattus rattus)
articles.abstract: Pre-habituation to the arena through repeated testing has been suggested to produce more robust and reproducible behavioural results. In this study, we investigated the effect of pre-habituation on odour discrimination and exploratory behaviour of wild-derived black rats (Rattus rattus). We subjected 66 black rats (26 males, 40 females) to two trials of an olfactory hole-board task in an enriched open field-like arena. We have found that black rats strongly prefer their species-specific odour over other odours (control, dried lemon balm, guinea pig). Moreover, the preference for conspecific odour seems to be detectable irrespective of variation in individuals' pre-habituation experience or inter-individual differences. Interestingly, we found that time spent inspecting the odour samples showed a distinctly different pattern than the number of visits to the odour samples, which may reflect individual interest in the odour and species-specific pattern of exploration, respectively. Both olfactory inspection and exploration were repeatable across trials, and we have found rather large inter-individual differences in some of the recorded behaviours, especially in vertical exploration (some animals consistently climb and rear more than others). Even though pre-habituation to the arena influenced both exploratory behaviour and the number of visits to the odour samples in the experiment, it did not alter the overall preference pattern for conspecific odour relative to the other odours. We conclude that the olfactory hole-board task is a reliable and repeatable method when testing olfactory discrimination, even in wild-derived animals.

articles.title: Unexpected male choosiness: Female aggressiveness as a criterion for mate choice preference in the red swamp crayfish
articles.abstract: As a core manifestation of sexual selection, mate choice preference has traditionally been studied primarily in the context of female assessment and selection of male traits, whereas active male choice for female phenotypic characteristics remains rarely reported in crustaceans. Among the various factors influencing mate choice outcomes, animal personality types-particularly aggressiveness-serve as key behavioural indicators of an individual's competitive ability and physiological condition. Here, using the red swamp crayfish (Procambarus clarkii), we investigated whether female aggressiveness influences male mate choice preference. After confirming sex effects on aggressiveness, we used a two-choice assay to examine the influence of female aggressive interactions and their outcomes on male preference. We found that sex affected fighting frequency: male-male pairs fought more frequently than female-female pairs, with male-female pairs intermediate. Male observers spent more time and made more entries into the winner zone than the loser zone and showed a positive standardized strength of preference (SOP), whereas female observers showed no such preference. Female aggression scores were positively correlated with male observers' duration in the preference zone. These findings suggest that male red swamp crayfish can assess the outcomes of fighting encounters between two females and prefer those females with a highly aggressive phenotype, revealing a reversal of conventional sex roles and providing new behavioral evidence for non-canonical sexual selection mechanisms in crustaceans.

articles.title: Yawning in lungfishes: occurrence and potential functional differences between respiratory modes
articles.abstract: Yawning is a stereotyped behavioural pattern observed across vertebrates and is considered multifunctional, but how its function changed during major physiological transitions remains poorly understood. Lungfishes provide an ideal model to address this question because species vary in their relative reliance on branchial and pulmonary respiration. We investigated whether yawning occurs in one individual each of the branchial-dominant Australian lungfish and three pulmonary-dominant species (marbled, spotted, and West African lungfishes) and, when present, characterized yawning frequency, yawning investment (frequency × duration), and activity levels before and after yawning. Yawning was observed exclusively underwater in all species. The branchial-dominant Australian lungfish showed a significantly higher yawning frequency than the three individual pulmonary-dominant lungfishes (negative binomial model: p = 0.007), whereas yawning investment was broadly comparable among the four individuals. In the branchial-dominant Australian lungfish, activity levels significantly increased following yawning (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p = 0.041), whereas no significant post-yawning increase was observed in the two pulmonary-dominant individuals. The magnitude of activity-level change associated with yawning differed significantly from that observed during control periods in the branchial-dominant Australian lungfish (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p = 0.006), but not when the pulmonary-dominant individuals were pooled. These observations indicate that lungfish yawning occurs underwater regardless of respiratory mode and is associated with differences in yawning characteristics and post-yawning activity among the individuals. Although these findings cannot establish species-level differences, they suggest that yawning function may vary with respiratory mode and warrant further comparative study.

articles.title: Pipeline for acoustic classification of ant (Formica rufa) behaviours: a suggested workflow for soil macrofauna studies
articles.abstract: Acoustic monitoring has been touted as an automatable monitoring technique to study the presence, activity or acoustic communication of soil animals. Yet current acoustic approaches have been criticized for lacking understanding of what soil fauna behaviours they are detecting. We investigate whether specific insect behaviours could be identified with sound by recording Red Wood Ants (Formica rufa) behaviours (running, struggling, biting and stridulation-like behaviour) with a contact microphone. We label recordings by hand, then extract two types of acoustic features, spectral and cepstral features, and show that most of the selected ant behaviours could be separated from each other based on their acoustic profiles. Based on our results, we propose an analytical workflow including principal component analysis as well as random forest classification that generates correct behavioural classifications in 67 to 90% of the sound snippets. Key features to separate behaviours include cepstral skewness, duration of sound events and mean frequency of the generated sound. Even if we encountered background noise, our pipeline could select relevant features from audio files and train a machine learning classifier. Our study demonstrates that acoustic features can be used to inform about specific insect behaviours and thus broaden the application of passive acoustic monitoring to species that do not communicate acoustically.

articles.title: Quantifying nonmnemonic strategies in two-alternative forced-choice delayed matching and nonmatching-to-position tasks in mice (Mus musculus) using automated video tracking technologies
articles.abstract: Delayed matching-to-position (DMTP) and delayed nonmatching-to-position (DNMTP) tasks are widely used as standard paradigms for evaluating working memory in rodents. In these tasks, which employ a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) design, animals initiate each trial by nosepoking a back key, which triggers the illumination of a sample key (either the left or right front key). Upon nosepoking the sample key, a delay begins. During this delay, the back key remains illuminated and animals may nosepoke it, but these responses have no programmed consequence. After the programmed delay, the first nosepoke on the back key activates both front keys. Reinforcement is contingent on choosing the same key as the sample in the DMTP task, or the opposite key in the DNMTP task. Performance is typically measured as the proportion of correct responses across varying delays, which generally decline as delay increases. However, whether the imposed mediating responses used in many protocols effectively prevents the use of nonmnemonic strategies remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we recorded and analyzed the movements of mice during these tasks using automated video tracking. Our findings suggest that mice may rely on nonmnemonic strategies, such as maintaining body position relative to the sample keys, rather than solely on working memory. These results challenge the assumption that DMTP and DNMTP tasks exclusively measure working memory, highlighting the need for cautious interpretation of task performance.

articles.title: Delay discounting of treatment outcomes by caregivers of children undergoing different behavior‐analytic interventions
articles.abstract: Outcomes of behavior-analytic interventions implemented with children can be mediated by the behavior of their caregivers, such as when they are called upon to implement treatments in natural settings. However, those outcomes are also often delayed, and humans have shown a decreased sensitivity to delayed reinforcement. This study replicated prior research on discounting of delayed treatment outcomes by caregivers of children receiving behavior-analytic interventions for dangerous or destructive behavior. It also compared sensitivity to delays by these caregivers with that of caregivers of children undergoing interventions focused on skill acquisition and to address food selectivity or refusal. Results demonstrated that caregivers of children receiving each type of behavior-analytic intervention discounted the value of delayed treatment outcomes. Caregivers of children undergoing intervention for dangerous or destructive behavior discounted the value of delayed treatment outcomes significantly more than those whose children were undergoing intervention focused on skill acquisition, indicating that immediacy was particularly important for those caregivers.

articles.title: Application of operant demand in autism and developmental disabilities: An updated review (2017–2025)
articles.abstract: Operant demand within behavioral economics provides a quantitative framework for evaluating reinforcer efficacy in applied research involving individuals with autism and those with related developmental disabilities. This systematic review extended the work of Gilroy, Kaplan, and Leader (2018) by examining applied operant demand research published between March 2017 and December 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, 30 articles (31 experiments; 307 participants) were identified and coded for procedural features and methods, including operant arrangements, demand and work output analyses, open and closed economies, and unit price applications. Results indicated increased use of demand and work output analyses and unit price applications. However, open and closed economies remained rarely evaluated and substantial variability was observed in procedural methods used to manipulate price. Findings indicate growing use of operant demand analyses for treatment durability and schedule thinning but continued underuse for generalization variables.

articles.title: Caregiver‐implemented standardized‐to‐individualized behavior‐analytic toilet‐training package for preschoolers with autism
articles.abstract: Children with autism often face challenges with incontinence and may benefit from more structured toilet training relative to neurotypical children. In the current study, we evaluated a standardized-to-individualized behavior-analytic toilet-training package with caregivers as the interventionists. We used telehealth to train caregivers remotely to support their implementation of the procedures and obtain additional data on implementation and outcomes. Four preschool-aged children with autism and their caregivers participated. Three of four participants met mastery criteria with a standardized toilet-training package and one participant required a contingent progressive sit schedule. Intervention components were successfully faded, and all participants maintained performance after 4 weeks. The findings demonstrate that clinic-based toilet-training procedures can be implemented at home by caregivers with telehealth support. This approach to toilet training provides families with an alternative to clinic-based treatment and could increase access to treatment among those residing in rural or underserved areas.

articles.title: Determining Learner‐Specific Prompt Type and Prompt‐Fading Procedures for Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT It is widely recognized that individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often require individualized educational programming. However, only a few studies have evaluated using an assessment to identify the most efficient and effective instructional components for individual learners. We replicated and extended previous research by conducting prompt‐type and prompt‐fading assessments with two adults with ASD to identify the most efficient prompt type (model, vocal‐gestural, or full physical) and prompt‐fading procedure (progressive prompt delay, most‐to‐least, or least‐to‐most). Following these assessments, we compared the most and least efficient procedures while evaluating whether the assessment results generalized to additional skill types. We also compared the assessment results to those of a decision‐making tool, the Systematic Worksheet for the Evaluation of Effective Prompting Strategies (SWEEPS). The most efficient prompt type was learner‐specific, whereas both participants learned most efficiently using a progressive prompt delay. These outcomes were replicated across additional functional skills and showed clear differences between the most and least efficient procedures. The assessment results were also consistent with the SWEEPS.

articles.title: Brief Access Delay and Interruption to Reduce Social Media Use: Is it Effective?
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Social media use is widespread among young adults, with many individuals frequently engaging with platforms that provide immediate access to entertainment, social interaction, and personalized content. Social media detoxification broadly refers to planned reductions, interruptions, or temporary restrictions in social media use. Few studies have experimentally evaluated the effects of specific access‐restriction strategies on social media use. The present study evaluated a brief access‐restriction intervention with five college students using a multiple‐baseline design. Access to each participant's two most frequently used social media applications was restricted using a mobile application that arranged time limits and brief delays to access, signaled by prompts. The primary dependent variable was the daily duration of use of the two targeted applications, measured via Screen Time reports generated by participants' phones. Results were mixed. Two participants demonstrated reductions in use, whereas the remaining participants showed minimal change or increases. These findings suggest that access restrictions alone may have limited effectiveness.

articles.title: A Review of Risk of Bias Assessments Within Literature Reviews and Meta‐Analyses Published in Behavior‐Analytic Journals
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Systematic literature reviews and meta‐analyses that follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines are commonly published within behavior‐analytic literature. One PRISMA guideline involves conducting a risk of bias assessment. Given the prevalence of PRISMA reviews in behavior‐analytic literature, evaluating how often this type of assessment is included within reviews may be useful. The purpose of this review was to identify the inclusion of risk of bias assessments as outlined by PRISMA in systematic literature reviews and meta‐analyses published within behavior‐analytic journals. Articles published between March 29, 2021, and March 31, 2026, were evaluated to assess the inclusion of this assessment since the most recent PRISMA guidelines published on March 29, 2021. For articles that included a risk of bias assessment, the quality of the assessment was also evaluated. Eighty articles met inclusion for this review and six included a risk of bias assessment. Across those six articles, quality scores ranged from 6/10 (partially aligned) to 8/10 (aligned), with an average score of 7 (aligned). These findings may help ensure that systematic reviews using PRISMA guidelines are conducted with consistency and quality. Future directions and implications of these results are discussed.

articles.title: Evaluating Video Modeling to Teach Caregivers to Conduct Paired Stimulus Preference Assessments
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Stimulus preference assessments have been shown to identify stimuli that are likely to function as reinforcers for individuals with disabilities. It is important to identify these stimuli to increase the effectiveness of interventions. The ability to conduct a stimulus preference assessment is a skill that caregivers should have; however, the research on training preference assessments is limited to staff, teachers, and students. The following study evaluated the effectiveness of video modeling to teach caregivers to conduct paired stimulus preference assessments. The results showed that video modeling was effective and that the results were maintained during a 1‐week follow‐up.

articles.title: A Comparison of Stimulus‐Stimulus Pairing and Operant Discrimination Training to Establish Conditioned Reinforcers
articles.abstract: ABSTRACT Individuals with developmental disabilities may be sensitive to a limited number of conditioned reinforcers. Stimulus‐stimulus pairing, a common strategy used to establish conditioned reinforcers, has demonstrated inconsistent results. Operant discrimination training involves conditioning reinforcers by presenting them as discriminative stimuli during operant conditioning. The effectiveness of establishing conditioned reinforcers using both methods was evaluated. Eight consecutively admitted individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities participated in the study. While both methods produced stimuli that induced above‐baseline levels of responding, only four participants demonstrated moderate‐to‐high treatment effects, and no relative advantage could be established for either procedure.

articles.title: Motivational and discriminative aspects of context in renewal and reinstatement of operant behavior in mice
articles.abstract: Renewal, reinstatement, and other forms of recovery of learned behavior after extinction have been interpreted in terms of the concept of context. Context is defined here as the field of stimuli that is interrelated with the behavior of an individual in the present. Two important classes of stimuli that comprise context are discriminative stimuli and motivating operations. Two experiments examined interactions between discriminative and motivational aspects of context in the renewal and reinstatement of operant behavior following extinction in mice. In Experiment 1, mice received all operant acquisition and extinction sessions under 24 hr of food deprivation. In Experiment 2, mice received half of acquisition and extinction sessions under 24 hr of deprivation and the other half under nondeprived conditions. In both experiments, mice were tested for renewal and reinstatement after extinction, one group under 24 hr of deprivation and the other nondeprived. Results showed that the extent to which recovery occurred depended on relations between motivating operations (a) during acquisition/extinction learning and (b) during tests for renewal and reinstatement. Translational implications for the study of recovery of behavior after extinction in nonlaboratory circumstances are discussed.

articles.title: Pavlovian Approaches to Preventing Impulsive Choice: Envisioning an Ideal School-Based Prevention Program
articles.abstract: Abstract Impulsive choice—preference for a smaller-sooner over a larger-later reward—is a transdiagnostic risk factor for behaviors that harm human health. Preventing a temporally extended pattern of impulsive choice should be a translational research priority. No existing intervention meets all the criteria outlined in this article of an ideal school-based prevention program: low cost, low teacher effort, fast-acting, and capable of producing lasting, generalizable reductions in impulsive choice. Here, we evaluate Pavlovian conditioning as a candidate approach. Our review is informed by evidence from nonhuman laboratory experiments and kindergarten classroom studies examining whether appetitive Pavlovian conditioning protocols can reduce impulsive choice and related behaviors. Laboratory experiments demonstrate that a brief Pavlovian conditioning protocol establishes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that may then be strategically used to reduce impulsive choice in rats by serving as an attractive antecedent and/or an appetitive delay-bridging stimulus. Studies conducted in kindergarten classrooms show that a class-wide protocol can establish an appetitive CS with minimal teacher training and classroom disruption. Presenting the CS during an in-situ waiting task reduced children's challenging behaviors and presenting it during academic-choice tasks increased children's willingness to work for larger rewards. This preliminary evidence supports the continued exploration of Pavlovian conditioning approaches to efficiently prevent patterns of impulsive choice that cumulate over time to negatively affect human health and wellbeing.

articles.title: Using Case-Specific Effect Sizes to Complement Visual Analysis in Single-Case Design Research
articles.abstract: Abstract Case-specific effect sizes have been developed to supplement the visual analysis of line-graphed data in single-case design research by quantitatively summarizing intervention effectiveness. This article provides background on case-specific effect sizes and describes when they can effectively complement visual analysis. We discuss several distinct families of case-specific effect size metrics, including nonoverlap indices (e.g., nonoverlap of all pairs), standardized measures (e.g., standardized mean difference), response ratios (e.g., percentage change), and goal attainment (e.g., percent of goal obtained). Furthermore, we discuss the assumptions and limitations that hold for all families of case-specific effect sizes and the assumptions and limitations of each type of case-specific effect size. In conclusion, we provide guidance for determining when these metrics are appropriate for a single-case design study and present a decision framework to help researchers select the most suitable effect size measure(s), if any, for their data.

articles.title: Type I Error in Single-Case Experimental Designs
articles.abstract: Abstract Type I errors, or false positives, occur when a researcher erroneously concludes that the independent variable caused a change in the dependent variable. Type I errors can result in resources being misused in both research and practice. Although Type I errors are most often associated with group design paradigms, researchers using single-case experimental designs are also susceptible to making Type I errors. In this article, we describe the research on Type I errors in single-case experimental designs across analytic methods, including visual analysis, machine learning, effect estimation, and randomization approaches. We also suggest ways that each analytic method can be used to mitigate Type I errors and highlight aspects of Type I error in single-case experimental designs that are understudied and in need of additional research.

articles.title: Quantifying Citation Diversity: A Clean Bib Tutorial
articles.abstract: The recent practice of including citation diversity statements in scholarly writing represents a movement toward transparency in citation practices. Among other things, the statement includes name-based classifications of first- and last-authors' demographics, most commonly gender and ethnicity, which can be estimated using application programming interfaces (APIs). In this tutorial, we outline how to use the Clean Bib tool to generate a citation diversity statement for the references cited in scientific and academic publications. Clean Bib uses GenderAPI and EthnicolrAPI to classify whether first and last author names are most likely names of men, women, white authors, or authors of color. Although it is limited in that gender and ethnicity are reduced to binary variables and other important demographic characteristics are excluded, it is an accessible and scalable tool to begin to examine perceived author characteristics and reflect on citation practices.

articles.title: Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s Disease Impairs Temporal Precision
articles.abstract: Abstract Several studies have reported temporal processing deficits in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease. These deficits can be quantified by interval timing paradigms that require participants to estimate or produce an interval of several seconds and require working memory for temporal rules as well as attention to time. Timing performance can be quantified by a variety of measures; however, two relatively universal metrics include: (1) temporal accuracy, defined as the mean temporal estimate and (2) temporal precision, reflected by the variability of temporal estimates. We examined temporal accuracy and precision in a meta-analysis of 14 studies in patients with Parkinson’s disease and 10 studies in patients with Alzheimer’s disease. It is striking that, in both diseases, temporal precision was reliably impaired across studies, whereas temporal accuracy was affected in Alzheimer’s but not Parkinson’s disease. Our meta-analysis suggests that despite the diversity of interval timing paradigms and the complexity of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, temporal precision is consistently impaired in these diseases. These results advance interval timing as a reliable assay to study cognitive dysfunction in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease and may extend to other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

articles.title: The Many Meanings of “Chaining”: A Historical Review and Proposal of a New Terminological Taxonomy
articles.abstract: Chaining procedures, initially developed through the experimental analysis of behavior, are now regularly investigated and implemented in applied behavior analysis research and practice. This article takes a deep dive into the history of applied chaining, presenting a qualitative review of the literature on this subject. Topics covered include guidelines for procedural implementation, lists of terms with multiple meanings and multiple terms with the same meaning, and a history of chaining within behavior analysis. This history sheds light on our current practices and highlights the need for certain changes. The culmination of this review is the proposal of a new set of terms related to chaining, intended for use by researchers and practitioners alike. The purpose of these suggested terminological revisions to our field’s verbal behavior is to provide greater clarity and structure to the taxonomy of terms used when speaking and writing about applied chaining.

articles.title: Serial Anticipation Learning in a Dashiell Maze: Speed and Variability to Reach the Goal
articles.abstract: This study investigated serial learning in albino rats subjected to a task that evaluated anticipatory behavior, behavioral variability, and serial learning in the Multiple Choice Maze proposed by Dashiell ( 1930 ). In the first phase, three consecutive reinforced trials (RRR type) were presented, followed by a second phase in which one group of rats faced an RNN type sequence, whereas another group faced an RNR type sequence. All subjects subsequently underwent a redetermination phase under RRR conditions. The results showed that rats exhibited anticipatory behavior, reducing their speed during no-rewarded trials but showing an increase in path variability. In general, the results successfully replicated previous studies on serial learning (Capaldi et al., 1990 ) and orientation behavior in mazes. In addition, new findings were identified, such as behavioral variability depending on the presence or absence of reinforcers and the time and distance of the runs in each trial. Taken together, this study contributes to the understanding of how organisms adapt and modify their behavior in response to environmental stimuli.

articles.title: An evaluation of behavior plan quality in Virginia’s developmental disability waiver system.
Behavioral Vaccine or Social Suppressant: The Good Behavior Game, a Scoping Review
articles.abstract: Arksey and O’Malley ( 2005 ) recommend that scoping review searches of the literature base should achieve both in-depth and broad results, rather than being guided by a highly focused research question (RQ). As such, we initially identified two broad RQs targeting the specific behavior of interest (RQ1) and the capture of unplanned mentions of this behavior within texts (RQ2). Owing to this breadth, the processes of scoping reviews are “not linear but iterative” (Arksey & O'Malley, 2005 , p. 22). Arksey and O’Malley expressly state their methodology “requir[es] researchers to engage with each stage in a reflexive way and, where necessary, repeat steps to ensure that the literature is covered in a comprehensive way” (p. 22). When our research team noticed social interactions frequently included within operational definitions, we added a third RQ to analyze this phenomenon and adjusted our final codebook to systematically explore this pattern. 1. How many studies explicitly target social interactions as a dependent variable? How many studies explicitly target social interactions as a dependent variable? 2. How many and to what extent do articles on the GBG mention unplanned anecdotal insights related to social interactions? How many and to what extent do articles on the GBG mention unplanned anecdotal insights related to social interactions? 3. How do studies include social interactions within operational definitions of target behaviors? a. Specifically, are increases or decreases in social interactions targeted? b. Are the dependent variables (DVs) that included social interactions intended to increase or decrease? c. On the basis of reported results, did the DVs that included social interactions increase or decrease as intended? How do studies include social interactions within operational definitions of target behaviors? a. Specifically, are increases or decreases in social interactions targeted? Specifically, are increases or decreases in social interactions targeted? b. Are the dependent variables (DVs) that included social interactions intended to increase or decrease? Are the dependent variables (DVs) that included social interactions intended to increase or decrease? c. On the basis of reported results, did the DVs that included social interactions increase or decrease as intended? On the basis of reported results, did the DVs that included social interactions increase or decrease as intended? We conducted searching and screening procedures in February 2024 using Academic Search Ultimate through EBSCO Host. We selected the following databases: Academic Search Ultimate, APA PsycINFO, Education Source, ERIC, and the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis through Wiley. We searched each database individually (not as a collection) and screened the results for duplicates using Zotero (Zotero, 2024 ). Our final search terms included: “Good Behavior Game” OR GBG OR “Caught Being Good Game” OR CBGG ensuring broad coverage. The initial searches yielded a total of 1006 articles across databases. We then limited results to peer reviewed academic journals in English resulting in 886 articles across databases (Academic Search Ultimate: n = 383; Education Source: n = 135; ERIC USU: n = 215; ERIC: n = 96; PsycINFO: n = 216; Jaba : n = 65). We conducted a first round of deduplication in Zotero, resulting in 527 articles. We then imported these articles ( n = 527) into Rayyan, a systematic literature review software (Ouzzani et al., 2016 ), where we removed an additional nine duplicate articles ( n = 518). From there, we removed author indexes, leaving a total of 499 studies for title and abstract screening. We did not limit the searches by year or geographical location. The screening process included: (1) title and abstract screening, (2) double screening and conflict resolution, (3) full text screening, and (4) full text conflict resolution. Figure 1 displays the PRISMA ScR flowchart. PRISMA Flow Chart To be included in the review, articles had to meet the following inclusion criteria: (1) Be a peer-reviewed, empirical study (training materials, intervention materials, opinion pieces, literature reviews were not included); (2) Be single subject or group experimental design; and (3) The title or abstract must mention the Good Behavior Game, GBG, Caught Being Good Game, or CBGG. We included all locations, date ranges, and settings in the initial screening. We excluded articles if the title or abstract stated an inter-dependent group contingency and not GBG specifically. Although common in GBG literature base, CW-Fit and Step-It-Up interventions are referred to as group contingencies separate from the GBG, so we excluded these variations. The first author trained researchers on screening articles using the above inclusion and exclusion criteria. A team of three researchers completed the first stage of article screening (title and abstract screening, n = 499), by selecting “yes,” or “no” within the Rayyan program (Ouzzani et al., 2016 ). If two researchers had a disagreement (e.g., one selected “yes” and the other selected “no”), researchers met as a team to review and screen the article to resolve the conflict. The first and third author double screened all included studies ( N = 499) and the fourth author triple screened a random 49% ( n = 254) of the sample. Throughout the title and abstract screening there were 28 conflicts, resulting in inter-rater reliability (IRR) of 95% and 142 articles moving to the full text screening stage. The first and second author double screened all articles at this level of screening ( n = 142; IRR = 90%) with 71 articles included for full text coding. We included texts for coding if social interactions by participants, as we defined them below, occurred anywhere in the text. We replicated the definition of social interactions from Walton, Preston, Hoffmann et al. ( 2026 ), that was originally adapted from Groves and Austin ( 2019 ): Positive peer interactions included verbalizations or statements aimed at encouraging peers, congratulating each other on performance (e.g., “That work is great,” “Well done!”), and requests or offers of assistance to one another. Positive physical gestures, which occurred when students were oriented to a peer and used motions such as thumbs up, waves, or high fives. Negative peer interactions included verbalizations or gestures that threatened, provoked, or demeaned a peer (e.g., name calling, laughing at peer mistakes, threatening to hit a peer), or interfering with a peer’s work (e.g., taking a peer’s book or materials). In accordance with Speltz et al. (1982), an interaction was considered directed toward a peer when the student used the peer’s name, their body was oriented toward the peer, or they had physical contact with the peer. (Walton, Preston, Hoffmann et al., 2026 , p. 6) The first and second author developed the codebook in Qualtrics with coders completing a survey for each article. Our team identified coding for group designs and single case designs on the same codebook was ineffective. We therefore split articles into single case ( n = 38) and group studies ( n = 33) with single case articles being coded for this paper. Group designs will be presented in a forthcoming paper. All single case studies ( n = 38) were double coded by the first and second author, with IRR of 93% agreement (range, 80% to 100%). At this stage, we identified the pattern of social interaction behaviors being included in larger operational definitions (meaning how behaviors targeted for change were described, they should be clear, concise, unambiguous, and objective; Cooper et al., 2020 ) and were repeatedly targeted for reduction. To understand this pattern more, we conducted additional coding of combined behavior classes (meaning the overall group, e.g., disruption), subclasses (meaning smaller behavior groups, e.g., verbal disruption and physical disruption folded into the main grouping of disruption), social topographies (examples of the behaviors under each class, e.g., hitting, talking to peers), and graphed variables for all articles identified as targeting behavior that included a social interaction. We then thematically coded behavior classes. Of these articles ( n = 27), 48.1% ( n = 13) were randomly selected for IRR with agreement of 92.5% (range, 72% to 100%). We exported all data from Qualtrics to Excel for analysis. We summarized all articles by the following features: experimental study design, location, participant demographics, school demographics, study purpose, intervention characteristics, dependent variable characteristics, and other reported outcomes. Single-subject designs were coded across the following designs: AB, ABAB reversal, variation of the ABAB reversal, alternating treatment design, multiple baselines across participants, multiple baselines across settings, variation of a multiple baseline (such as an embedded reversal), multi-element design, multiple probe design, or other. Our team collected information regarding the country of implementation as well as geographic region. Geographic region included information such as rural, urban, suburban, or not reported to identify reporting standards within the literature base. We coded for multiple participant characteristics, including total number of participants reported broken down into number of students, number of teachers, and number of schools. Researchers coded for participant age range and/or grade range and classroom type, which included options such as general education, special education resource room, special education self-contained/small group/Pupil Referral Units (PRU; British special education schools for US equivalent of Emotional and Behavioral disability [EBD]), special education additional services such as applied behavior analysis (ABA) clinic, camp, ABA lab, residential/hospital, or other school setting such as cafeteria or hallway. Finally, researchers coded for any reported disability classification including ASD/autism, ADHD/ADD, specific learning disability (SLD), intellectual disability (ID), EBD, oppositional defiance disorder (ODD), behavioral disorder, and/or speech language impairment (SLI). When a disability classification was encountered but not listed, the codebook was adjusted to account for this. We charted these data using frequency tables, binary frequency tables, and we assessed how disability reporting varied across setting and grade level using Excel filtering. The research team coded a variety of school-level variables. These included school type, such as elementary/middle/high/post-secondary, residential, charter, or pre-school. Additional coded variables included the percentage of students receiving free and reduced-price lunch (FRPL), percentage of students receiving Individualized Education Plan (IEP) services, Title 1 status, and the percentage of students reported as English second language (ESL) students. We synthesized data across binary frequency tables representing percentage of articles that did or did not report each variable. Researchers coded the reported aims of each study including: comparison of game variations, comparison of the GBG intervention with another intervention, outcomes of the GBG on secondary non-targeted behaviors, behavior reduction, behavior increase, both behavior increase and decrease, component analysis of different intervention features. We numerically analyzed these data within a table to identify patterns of aims. Researchers coded a variety of intervention characteristics. We reported if the intervention used was the GBG or the CBGG. Included game rules were coded as providing the full list, only examples, or failed to report rules entirely. We also reported if the studies provided rationale for the selection of the rules, and if the rules of the intervention were aligned with the targeted DVs. We analyzed these data for frequency of responses, characteristic overlap, and study aim overlap. For coding of the DV characteristics, we first identified if the included studies targeted a social interaction as either (a) its own response class, meaning social interaction behaviors were their own DV; or (b) if a social interaction was included as part of a combined DV or combined response class. All DVs with inclusion of social interactions were coded for purpose; options included: targeted for increase, decrease, both, or general observable effects, and researchers reported the provided definition. Of the studies that included social interactions as part of a larger dependent variable, we coded the name of the combined class, all subclasses, and all social topographies; these were then thematically grouped. Finally, our team coded if studies included a psychometric tool that included a form of student social outcome or if any anecdotal reporting of student social interactions was reported within articles. We summarized our analysis and synthesis by charting data across frequency tables in Excel, heat maps, binary frequency tables displaying percentage of occurrence across articles to account for varied sample sizes across educational settings. Table 1 presents our data on publication outlets. The majority of articles included in this review were published in the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (39.5%; n =15). Followed by the Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions (10.5%; n = 4). Twelve other journals were included with the majority publishing either one or two articles. These distribution data indicate the GBG studies that included social interactions have a wide audience and reach, with many journals focusing on research in schools and behavior intervention support. The year of publication for each article is represented in Fig. 2 and these range from 1969 to 2022. Publication of articles on the GBG that included social interactions significantly increased after 2011, with 31.6% ( n = 12) being published between 2020 and 2022, indicating an increasing trend of social interactions being included within publications in some form. Frequency of Articles Published Across Decades The articles included in this review were largely published from within the USA (81.6%; n = 31). The UK represented 10.5% ( n = 4) of the articles, and other European countries represented 7.9% ( n = 3) of the articles. Figure 3 shows most of the research in this area is focused within the USA. articles.title: Self-Censorship and Rule Governed Behavior
articles.abstract: Abstract This essay analyzes faculty self-censorship behavior amid political interference in Florida public higher education. Political interference increasingly regulates faculty behavior through statutes, administrative policies, and institutional directives that alter teaching, research, and scholarly discourse. We examine faculty self-censorship as rule-governed behavior using an established taxonomy of rules (Pelaez, 2013; Pelaez & Moreno, 1998) as its primary theoretical framework. The taxonomy articulates five interacting dimensions of rules: (a) explicitness, (b) accuracy (correspondence), (c) complexity, (d) source, and (e) temporal relations. These five dimensions are used to explore how legal and organizational rule systems influence individual faculty behavior under conditions of political intimidation. Recent concepts from higher education and political philosophy scholarship, including anticipatory obedience and repressive legalism, are integrated within this behavior-analytic framework. Florida’s public higher education system and the Eleventh Circuit’s decision affirming the injunction against the Stop WOKE Act serve as a contemporary case study illustrating how ambiguous, incongruent, and externally imposed rules may generate self-censorship despite changing legal contingencies.

articles.title: Navigating the Unpaved Path to Behavior Analysis and Social Issues: Reflections from Early-Career Scholars
articles.abstract: Students interested in applying behavior analysis to social issues, advocacy, and systems-level change often encounter unclear professional pathways during training. Although behavior analysis provides a strong foundation for understanding behavior, many students interested in culturo-behavior science (CBS) and social justice-related work receive limited formal guidance on how to pursue these interests within existing training models. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences navigating behavior analysis and social issues as students and early-career professionals. We discuss barriers related to coursework, practicum experiences, interdisciplinary collaboration, mentorship, and professional identity development while pursuing values-aligned work both within and outside traditional behavior-analytic spaces. We also offer recommendations for students interested in advocacy-oriented and culturally responsive applications of behavioral science, including strategies for identifying resources, building collaborative communities, and sustaining momentum while navigating uncertain professional pathways. Our goal is to provide guidance and encouragement for students seeking to engage in socially responsive and systems-level applications of behavior analysis.

articles.title: An Initial Investigation of the Implementation, Effects, and Social Validity of a Mathematics Vocabulary Intervention
articles.abstract: Abstract This study examines the implementation, effects, and social validity of an explicit systematic mathematics vocabulary (MV) intervention for students with learning disabilities or difficulties. Participants included 30 students ages 11–14 who demonstrated a lack of mastery of third-grade MV and were assigned to treatment or control groups within classes. The two groups were similar at pretest in mathematics achievement and MV; however, the treatment group ( M = 42.6, adjusted M = 42.4) significantly outperformed the control group ( M = 34.1, adjusted M = 34.3) on the MV posttest ( b = 8.15, p < .001, 95% CI [5.30, 11.01], g = 1.99, adjusted g = 1.80). Observational data show teachers implemented the intervention with acceptable levels of fidelity. Social validity data suggest teachers found the intervention acceptable and easy to use. Results of this study suggest well-designed explicit, systematic instruction can produce positive effects when teaching MV to students requiring intensive MV intervention.
