articles.title: Laterality in toe-tapping behaviour of green-and-black poison dart frogs (Dendrobates auratus)
articles.abstract: Laterality, the preference for using one side of the body over the other, has been observed in various animal species, including frogs and toads. While laterality has been studied widely during locomotion in anurans, its role during other behaviours, such as hunting-related toe-tapping (the quick up and down movement of the middle toe of the hind feet while foraging), remains largely unstudied. This study investigated the toe-tapping rate of the left and right toes (versus both toes simultaneously) in a captive colony of green-and-black poison dart frogs (Dendrobates auratus, Dendrobatidae). We assessed the time spent tapping with each toe (right, left, or both toes simultaneously) in response to prey-mimicking videos, based on behavioural observations of 25 individuals. Simultaneous toe-tapping was rare, and laterality tests showed that frogs had an overall preference to toe-tap with their right toes (i.e., most individuals are right-lateralised) when presented with visual artificial prey. Since anurans prefer to strike at their prey once it is apparent in their right visual field, predator-prey interaction on the predator's right body side (i.e., with its right toe) might be beneficial for the predator, and a potential clue towards a better understanding of the function of hunting-related toe-tapping in frogs.

articles.title: Song modulation and auditory feedback under different behavioral contexts in adult male Bengalese finches
articles.abstract: Birdsongs are classified into two types based on behavioral context: undirected song (US) and directed song (DS). Comparisons of US and DS following manipulations of auditory feedback have provided insights into the mechanisms underlying adult song plasticity and maintenance. When deafened as adults, the US of the Bengalese finch changes more rapidly than that of other species (e.g., zebra finch and budgerigar). However, it remains unclear whether the DS of Bengalese finches undergoes similarly rapid degradation. In this study, we deprived adult male Bengalese finches of auditory input and conducted long-term comparisons of US and DS following deafening. We examined the ratios of the number of higher syllables to that of low syllables (H/L) to characterize both US and DS at each time point before and after deafening. After deafening, the decrease in H/L emerged significantly faster and greater in US than in DS. The syllable sequence stereotypy score was lower in US than in DS at 7-14 days after deafening. These findings demonstrate that in adult Bengalese finches, auditory deprivation induces greater alteration more rapidly in US than in DS. We discuss the possibility that differences between US and DS arise from distinct neural activity patterns in the anterior forebrain pathway, which is involved in song learning and modification.

articles.title: Motor planning in Colombian spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps rufiventris)
articles.abstract: The morphological constraint hypothesis suggests that primates with less dexterity show more consistent motor planning because there is less flexibility to compensate for inefficient actions. Spiders monkeys offer a unique opportunity to test this hypothesis because they do not have a functional thumb. Colombian spider monkeys (Ateles fusciceps rufiventris, n = 8) housed at a wildlife park were tested on a standard motor planning task. A trial began when a dowel baited on one end was placed on an elevated apparatus and ended when a monkey grasped the dowel with the hands. Grip use was coded from video as radial (pronated overhand grip with the radius bone towards food) or non-radial. The percentage of radial grips was used in analyses for comparison to other platyrrhines. As a group, spider monkeys used a radial grip significantly more than chance (M ± SD=73.38% ± 18.91), indicating spider monkeys engage in second-order motor planning. Spider monkeys differed in radial grip use from captive cotton-top tamarins (Saguinus oedipus) but not captive (Sapajus spp) or wild capuchins (Sapajus libidinosus) tested on the elevated dowel task in prior work by other investigators. Together, these findings have mixed implications for the morphological constraint hypothesis that merit further study.
